utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's Colonel Stutt, I think?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Colonel Stutt, we speak the same language, and there is a problem there for -- with ensuring that we go slowly enough for the interpreters. There will be a pause between your answers and my next question, while I ensure they have caught up. Are you a career Canadian soldier with some 33 or more years experience? Your career is set out in the first two paragraphs of the summary that's been provided to the Court and the Defence; that summary showing, amongst other things, that you joined the ECMM monitors in August '93, joining team 4, having responsibility for Zepce, Zavidovici, Breza and Vares, becoming its team leader at the end of September. Thereafter, taking over from Philip Watkins as the head of CC Travnik on the 17th of October, and from Sir Martin Garrod as the head of the RC Zenica in May '94, eventually leaving for Belgium in August, '94?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your first visit to Zepce, was that on the 4th of September of '93, following a reported incident of a mine, and did you make that visit in the presence of Christine Amnanpour from CNN to consider HVO allegations of considerable damage and deprivation in Zepce?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you find?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: We found that Zepce wasn't exactly what we had been led to expect, in terms of the fact that there was in fact power, enough to eat, gasoline was available and other consumables, to a much greater degree than we had been led to believe. And, of course, this caused us to conclude that Zepce was getting sustenance from somewhere else, probably from the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thereafter, was access to the -- for the ECMM to Zepce controlled by Colonel Blaskic from his headquarters in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning to Vares. On the 1st of October, did you meet Zvonko Duznovic, the police chief for Vares?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he tell you something about apparent HVO and BSA intentions in relation to a village close to Vares?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've put the little map with which the Chamber is familiar on the ELMO. Point out the village concerned and its location, please, to Stupni Do and Vares, and say what you were told.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, I can't find Zepce on this map, but I know where it is, because Stupni Do is here and that village is south and slightly east.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you use the pointer just to show the Judges. There we are. Stupni Do is highlighted in green, and the other village --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, your microphone, please. Interpreters cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. The other village, of which you were told, is called what?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other village?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Zizci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back. Just leave the map where it was, please. I think on the 1st of October you saw Zvonko Duznovic, and did he say something about -- about something that was going to happen to another village?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Zvonko said that there had been a report that there would be an attack on the village of Zizci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who did he say that attack was going to be by?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: He said it was going to be an attack by both the HVO and the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's all my fault for mishearing what word you are using. It's Zizci. And if we look at the map again, leaving it exactly on its present place on the ELMO, Zizci is a couple of kilometres south-east of Stupni Do. Now, in due course we know what happened at Stupni Do. Did you at some stage wonder whether there was any connection between Zizci and Stupni Do or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I did, because there were a number of villages in that area, and by reputation it was claimed that a great deal of black market racketeering was going on. So it's possible there could have been a similarity in the activities in those two villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on to the 9th of October. Did you learn, Colonel Stutt, of the attitude of a man called Ivica Rajic to the proposed repair of the Kiseljak-Visoko road, which was then in a state of disrepair?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes. At that time he wasn't supportive of fixing that particular road, and the assumption then would be so they could use the road that went through Bilalovac and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Briefly, could you see any logic in the HVO wanting to enforce the using of the Bilalovac-Busovaca road in preference to the Kiseljak-Visoko road or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes. If you can't use the Kiseljak-Visoko road, you have an opportunity to repair a secondary route you may need at other times for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the event, did Blaskic intervene or make a decision about repair of the road?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes. Eventually, the road was fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a small-ish collection of documentary exhibits in chronological order. If they haven't been distributed already, may they be distributed, please, to the Bench and to the Defence? The witness already has a collection in the same order in front of him. Perhaps if we can proceed in the way that has sometimes been helpful, if the witness can look at his own documents on the desk and the usher can simply lay the appropriate documents on the ELMO as we come to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Colonel Stutt, did you, on the 17th of October, succeed Philip Watkins in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that day, did you meet Dario Kordic, Exhibit 1249 --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- being your report, as we can see from the second sheet of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first entry on the first page sets out the title that you associated with him. How did the title that you have there for him come about?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's the position that he held as described to me, and it was at the time the way we were introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He made the following points, A to -- well, it's AA, B and C, actually -- that the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan offered the most hope for peace, that Muslim leaders were not in a hurry to obtain a lasting peace because they believed that time was on their side, particularly compared to Serbia affected by sanctions, and he expressed the view or made the point that the Muslims would suffer for one more winter. He made the point that the military objective of the BiH in the Vitez pocket was not for victory but to inflict casualties and seize ground, little by little, and then made the point that HVO commanders and politicians had been directed to assist in any way possible the Convoy of Joy based on a supposition that future convoy would be dedicated to the Croats in the Lasva Valley. That's your note. Incidentally, the exclamation mark beside that is, I think, not your annotation and has been put on at some more later time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you remember where you met him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes. It was the first time I had met Mr. Kordic, and I met him at what we referred to as the dacha in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that the lodge some kilometres up a country lane or road?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you remember now how he was dressed, or surrounded, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I can't remember on that day if Mr. Kordic was wearing civilian clothes or a uniform, but he was with a number of aides, and it was the first time that I had met Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 20th of October, Exhibit 1254.1 comes next, you received a report that the Kiseljak-Visoko road had been repaired. You also learned of six soldiers apparently captured -- six BiH soldiers apparently captured by the HVO in Vares close to a checkpoint, this being a matter of concern. And as we see on the document, 1254.1, your report for the 20th of October, two thirds of the way down the first sheet you report this: "The village of Stupni Do is an isolated, undefended, but completely surrounded Muslim village which has been remarkably spared from the ravages of war. It has been existing as a nearly untroubled Muslim suburb of HVO Vares. This is either a case of Stupni Do troops breaking some unwritten rule or it's another indicator of military tension in the Vares area of responsibility." How did this arrest of six soldiers fit with the previous level of cooperation between Muslims and Croats in Vares?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It surprised me, because I had visited Stupni Do a week or so previously and it was very, very loosely protected by, at that point, by my count, six uniformed BiH soldiers with very little in the way of weaponry, and it was a very, very casual place. The first report said that they had been arrested during one of the regular shopping visits, and that they often shopped in Vares, and this was most unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 9 of the summary. The 23rd of October of '93, did you receive a report from Oscar Meijboom that their team of monitors had been held up at a BiH checkpoint because of fighting going on in Stupni Do and Vares?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 24th of October, did you get first reports of an alleged massacre in Stupni Do, coming from the Vares government in exile, and did you send monitors, including Weckesser, who reported smoke from the village to which access was blocked by HVO checkpoints, they also reporting that there had been three military HVO vehicles leaving Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was your interim conclusion as to what the vehicles from Stupni Do might have been carrying?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Stupni Do had been described as a location where there was a great deal of black market racketeering. The first assumption is that the vehicles might well have been carrying contraband material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that ever confirmed on reports one way or another?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It was never confirmed one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed was there ever any discovery of which you were aware in Stupni Do of supplies of tobacco or alcohol or whatever else was on the black market?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: None of which I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document, 1259, paragraph 11. The second page of that document, paragraph 7, you said that under the assessment of Vares, that its complexities were well noted. It had been calm, with Stupni Do untouched. You went on to record or report a rift between HVO Vares and the displaced HVO from Kakanj, and you expressed the view that the Vares chief of security, Zvonko Duznovic, had influence beyond his position and had been identified on both sides as a cause of problems in the area?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this time was Emil Harah granting or denying access?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Granting access.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, he was granting access?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are we talking about Stupni Do now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, he was not granting access. He said it was unsafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the BiH commander in the area, Nehru Ganic, what was his attitude?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: He was very, very concerned, first of all, for the safety of the people in Stupni Do, and later for the Muslim population in Vares itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at that time the route for humanitarian aid to Tuzla, was that through Vares, and was that the only route?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It might not have been the only route, but it was the only main route.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So what pressure was there to keep that route open?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: We thought there would be great pressure to maintain the status quo that existed, which is one of the reasons we believed Vares had, up till that point, been a very quiet place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think if we look at the first page of the same exhibit, 1259, towards the bottom of the first page we see Ganic is spoken of, and he complains of the inability to protect the Muslims, and set a 1500 hours deadline to gain access, saying that, absent that, there would be retaliation. He also said that only 21 of 220 Muslims had escaped from Stupni Do. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move to the 25th of October and the next Exhibit 1263. On the 25th, did you learn of a denial of access to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You learned of a meeting between Sir Martin Garrod and Kordic, and were you aware of an allegation from a witness to the effect that the HVO were acting in self-defence, although you were able to form a view on that general topic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I was. As a result of my visit to Stupni Do, before the tragic events that happened in Stupni Do, I mentioned previously a very, very loosely garrisoned, well-fed community. But most importantly, there was no sign inside Stupni Do of fortification or any of the signs of a military build-up, or any sign of artillery or any type of weapon above and beyond the personal weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at 1263, on the first page under the heading "political." The second paragraph sets out the claim that the HVO was acting in self-defence, and your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I had a great deal of difficulty believing that HVO Vares was under any threat from anything I had seen in the village of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the foot of the page we have the paragraph that begins with the reference to denial to Stupni Do, but the last four lines of it set out how the local Red Cross were able to inform you of the incarceration of Muslim males in the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then over the page at the top, you were by now being informed, that's the 25th of October, the top two lines, of Kresimir Bozic having apparently replaced Emil Harah?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you ever able to verify whether these were genuine replacements, one person by another, or of when they occurred?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly when they occurred, but Emil Harah had been replaced prior to the final evacuation of the Bobovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But as to any changes before the attack on Stupni Do, were you ever able to verify one way or another whether such changes in personnel relieving them of responsibility had, in fact, occurred before that date?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, I could not confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 13 of the summary, the 26th of October. Were you briefed by NordBat following their interviews of Muslims who had escaped from Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the general allegation coming from those Muslims was that the place had been attacked, burned, men had been shot and women raped?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What had happened to the survivors?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Imprisoned in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document is 1266.1, your report for the 26th of October. Did you learn, as recorded there, of Muslim men being incarcerated before the attack on Stupni Do; they being held in elementary schools?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we look at the second page of this exhibit, and at the top of it, we see a general account of the allegations made via NordBat at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Generally, was there any information coming to you about members of the HVO in the Vares area who may have helped Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes. Several sources reported that in some cases HVO soldiers in Vares had protected some of the Muslims who were their friends. Equally, it was pointed out that somebody in Vares, who knew where the Muslims lived, had to identify those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next exhibit, 1261. This is a document signed by Petkovic, dated the 24th of October, apparently being a ceasefire. Comment, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: This document was understood by us at the time to be very much of an after-the-fact event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Connected to, in any way, the events that were unfolding in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Certainly, and more than likely as a result of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any substance in this being a real and new ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: We certainly didn't think it was anything new. We thought it was a reaction to the obvious event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you concerned, one way or another, about whether at this stage there was any reprimand or dismissal for those involved in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Certainly, we expected something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it known or believed who was in charge of the events that led to the massacre of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: The name Rajic appeared from all of our sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was any step taken -- sorry, I mustn't go too fast. Any step taken by this stage to discipline or dismiss that man?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: His name didn't appear on the document of those who were to be relieved as a result of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 16. The 27th of October had NordBat and the ECMM gaining access to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We turn, paragraph 17, to Exhibit 1293.2. The first page, second paragraph, has your meeting Dario Kordic, described as vice-president of the HVO government, and Valenta, vice-president of the HDZ. Asked about the future of Croats in Middle Bosnia, Kordic said that Boban's heart was in Central Bosnia and that he would cut his heart out before surrendering it, and that the HVO would fight to the last man to defend the three HVO pockets of the Lasva Valley, Kiseljak, Kresevo and Zepce. The next comment: "HVO in Vares had been accustomed to a lifestyle of smuggling and must not be compared to the HVO elsewhere." Whose comment was that, yours or Kordic's?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That was Mr. Kordic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You went on to say that immediate BiH intentions were to capture Zepce to split the pocket between Novi Travnik and Busovaca, to take Kiseljak, and finally to return and deal with Vitez?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he said they were organised, equipped and armed. Now, that was, I think, the first part of a two-part meeting. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I met privately with Mr. Kordic and his staff prior to the much larger meeting which was attended by a representative of BH command and a senior representative of UNHCR. The purpose of this meeting was to deal with a threat that had been made publicly by Mr. Rajic to a UNHCR protection officer. As a result of that, UNHCR suspended their operations in Kiseljak. Something had to be done to return the status quo. So the second part at the much larger meeting, Mr. Kordic announced that Mr. Rajic was being replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And do we see that meeting noted at the foot of the first page, where you say he met with a delegation from the UNHCR and UNPROFOR; Rajic is dealt with with a great deal of reasonableness all around, and then Kordic noted that good and honest men occasionally give in to stress; the issue would be dealt with tomorrow, and so on? Now, the conclusion that you drew from that about the line of authority for Rajic was what?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It was very clear, in order to fire someone, that person has to work for you. Mr. Kordic was seen to be Mr. Rajic's superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there anything in that meeting said by him or by anyone else to suggest that anybody else had the relevant authority?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exhibit is a very short part of a long video. The video number is 1280. The transcript, which I don't know that the witness has, is 1280.1. I hope I've had it queued at the right place, but it doesn't matter if I haven't. I'll explain the position. The video starts with a televised press conference of Kordic, Kostroman and the interviewer, but at page 8 of the transcript -- I beg your pardon -- page 7 of the transcript, we see, three quarters of the way down the page, the interviewer speaking of an opportunity to talk to the first man of Central Bosnia, and I understand that to be a telephone interview. And if we turn over now to page 8, halfway down, we come, right in the middle of the page, to the one short passage that I want this witness to deal with, for in the interview, the interviewer and Kordic are dealing with the meeting on the 9th of November with which we've just been dealing. I haven't had a chance this morning to check that it's queued at the right place. I know how very difficult it is to queue things from tapes. Can we try it, and if not, we'll just live with the written transcript? So if they could just play it and see if we're at the right place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop that. Thank you very much. If necessary, we can return to find it on the monitor after the break. But for the time being, the video having been provided, we'll proceed on the transcript. If the witness has that at page 8, we see that in a recorded interview, an interviewer has said to Mr. Kordic: "You were the first to promptly suspend the decision of Ivica Rajic, the commander from Kiseljak, who banned the work of the UNHCR. What is the situation?" The first question, Colonel, do you understand that to be a reference to the meeting with which you've just dealt?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reply goes as follows: "In any case, on the day this decision was issued, the most responsible leaders of Croatian Central Bosnia immediately organised a meeting with the highest officials of the UNHCR and UNPROFOR based in Kiseljak. That meeting was organised in Busovaca, and I think that it ended in complete success to the mutual satisfaction of both sides." And then it goes on. Your comment, please, on his then response to a question about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes. What follows in the transcript is not what the focal point of the meeting was about. The meeting really was a one-agenda meeting to deal with the difficulty of Mr. Rajic having threatened the UNHCR protection officer, and the announcement that the decision had been taken to replace Mr. Rajic was the really single agenda issue of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does Mr. Kordic ever respond directly to the question by the interviewer that he was the first promptly to suspend the decision of Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Not that I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exhibit, 1311. On the 18th of November, your report, I think. We see on the first page that you met Blaskic, and comments are there set out about Kordic's position. From where did they come; from Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely, that he was Mate Boban's vice-president for Middle Bosnia, although for procedural reasons, it may take some time before his appointment could be confirmed, it was said. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Blaskic told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The block of text ends, "All sources questioned have said the same thing, Valenta is finished, but Kordic remains the major HVO influence in Middle Bosnia." How did that fit or otherwise with your own view on his role?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That confirmed what a number of other sources told me, and that was my view at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think at the top of the second page we see the record of your meeting with Pero Skopljak, who said he did not think HVO enclaves would hold out -- HVO enclaves would hold out without external intervention. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But he also made it clear that the HVO ambition was to link Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And thus to Herzegovina. Next exhibit is 1315. So far as Rajic is concerned, what was his position? Did he remain in some position of authority?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: He was replaced in his actual position, but he remained on, we were told, by all concerned as an adviser. And, in any event, remained the major player in the Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that if we look at the -- you ought really, I suppose, to go to the second exhibit first, 1297, which is the 11th of November. You see on the second page under paragraph 7 the first expressed seeming belief, "It seems that Rajic has been replaced because of his attitude towards UNHCR. This can cause another internal problem in Kiseljak, since Rajic has a sort of private army." But the other exhibit, 1315, dated the 22nd of November, records, at the foot of the first page, that he remains on location as an adviser. The evidence you've just given us.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he also recorded as having these paramilitary groups called the Apostoli, Maturice?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reputation of those units and their function being to what effect?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Acting as a private army, group of bandits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What sort of things did -- were they alleged to have done?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: By repute, control of the black market.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was your overall conclusion about the alleged removal of Rajic; was it genuine or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: The issue of some kind of a public order had to happen in order that the problem with UNHCR could be seen to be dealt with. But most people understood that Mr. Rajic was important enough that as long as he was still in the area, he would be still in control of much of what took place in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As we've heard already, following the Stupni Do attack, the BiH took over the Vares pocket at the beginning of November, '93, the Bobovac Brigade abandoning and burning their headquarters when they left.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 1331. On the 15th of December of 1993, did you meet Blaskic, at the foot of the first page recorded, to ask him about the status of Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say that he had met Kordic earlier in the afternoon, and neither of you were left in any doubt about Kordic's importance in Middle Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You record, four lines up from the bottom of the page, "Blaskic added that Kordic had been many places and done many things, and that his position of influence was assured."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You went on to say that the assembly on the 23rd of December would make Kordic's official position clearer. And over the page, at a meeting you then had with Maric, he said that Kordic was an official delegate to the government of Central Bosnia, but had refused to accept the position of minister in order to better serve the inhabitants of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next exhibit, 1376. On the 16th of February, did you meet Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Top of the page in this report. Did you discuss the newly inaugurated parliament in Sarajevo, to which Kordic's response was what?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That it was a non-legitimate body, it wouldn't stand the test of time, and would become irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you just turn over, please, to the second page, subparagraph -- not subparagraph, "V1 discussed with Dario Kordic." Now, is that the same meeting or a different meeting? You haven't been pointed to it earlier. Don't guess. Any recollection or not at the moment?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I can't recall if the team was with me that day. My guess would be that they weren't, because I normally saw Mr. Kordic by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll move onto the next exhibit. Paragraph 23 on the summary. Did you meet again with Kordic in Busovaca on the 21st of March, by which time Boban had resigned. And we can see your comments underlined indeed at the first page of Exhibit 1404, where you say that his real position had been uncertain, but that he had lately been emphasising his position as a HVO Colonel. You expressed your view about his being the most influential Croat in Middle Bosnia, although under some challenge from the president of Zepce. And you said, "It's apparent that Kordic is calling all the HVO shots." The last sentence, perhaps you would just like to read it. Read it out to us and explain its derivation, the sentence beginning with "initiatives for peace and goodwill."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: "While goodwill and peace initiatives were going on elsewhere. Kordic remained more hardlined and anti-Muslim."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you explain how you formed all of that, that view?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I formed that opinion over a long period of time, not at any one specific meeting, based on my realisation that Mr. Kordic's relationship with the BiH would be very much unrelenting, unbending and unflexible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By this stage, what initiatives, peace and goodwill, were there available to be built on?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Well, we were looking at the start-up of the Washington Agreement, and places where there had been absolutely no progress at all in the past were suddenly starting to loosen up. For instance, routes between Zepce and Zavidovici. There was a great deal of interest in getting humanitarian through routes, that humanitarian aid hadn't been able to get through before. And, frankly, we were surprised at the potential rapid progress of the peace process.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How, if at all, did Kordic embrace the possibility of speedy resolution?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic's attitude was, consistently and throughout, that we had to take one thing at a time, that there were bad memories on all sides, and that progress, because of this, must be very slow. In fact, events caused things to move more quickly than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you attend a meeting with -- at the Hotel Vitez on the 4th of April with Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that's Exhibit 1410. Have you got that before you? I think it's at the second page, if you look over to the second sheet. Tell us what Kordic said then about the Federation parliament and so on.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: As the Federation parliament moved forward, and it relates to the meeting that Mr. Kordic had with President Tudjman, following his meeting with President Tudjman he became much more flexible about progress between the two communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you infer or interpret from what he told you about the meeting with Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It was my --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and its reality?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It was my opinion he had been read the riot act and publicly be seen to do those things that he had been ordered to do, but we didn't expect progress any faster than Mr. Kordic could control it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been speaking about the Easter meeting. I think, in fact, you've been speaking from memory and probably haven't got the document before you. It doesn't matter. If you have, you may not have had it open, but don't worry about that. You've provided what I wanted. On the 20th of May -- this is Exhibit 1423, the second-to-last exhibit -- did you meet again Kordic in Busovaca when he was dressed how?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: He was dressed in uniform and explained that he had been promoted to the rank of brigadier in the reserves. However, this rank and position would be largely ceremonial, since his main focus would be to remain on political events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see here, on the first page of Exhibit 1423, in the first paragraph, he setting out his recent visit to President Tudjman, along with the mayors of Central Bosnia, and maintained that he was pleased with the solution reached at the Vienna talks about self-governed Croat municipalities?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That is correct, and if I was out of sequence here, I believe it was at that meeting that I formed the opinion that Mr. Kordic's public image was changing a little as a result of his meeting with Mr. Tudjman and that he had, no doubt, been read some form of riot act.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going back to the Easter meeting, perhaps we should just make sure you've got 1410 in front of you, and it may not be in your stack because you haven't brought a stack with you. It's the second sheet of -- the second page of 1410, top of the page, the Easter meeting. In response to a question, Dario Kordic says: "As the Bosnian Federation Parliament grows, the CRHB will devolve out of existence." Is this the discussion you had with him?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He went on to say it wouldn't happen immediately because it would be quite a while before the question of canton boundaries was sorted out, and he predicted the autumn before the Serbs would take it seriously?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then 1429.1, the last exhibit, deals with the week of the 12th to the 18th of June. We see on the third page that President Tudjman had visited the Croats of Central Bosnia. I think you met Mr. Kordic shortly after that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, that was the meeting where Mr. Kordic explained to me that he had been promoted to the rank of brigadier in the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did he say that he would be working mainly with the party of the HDZ in the cantons?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just, I think, one or two other questions. You've already explained how you formed your view about Kordic, but what was your approach to him in order to have the benefit of relaxed conversations with him; how did you treat him?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I always treated Mr. Kordic amicably. He treated me the same way. I met infrequently with him in Busovaca throughout the period of the year that I spent in Middle Bosnia. I was told when I first got there that Mr. Kordic was, in fact, the single most important Croat person in Middle Bosnia, and during the course of the year that I spent there, that opinion was reinforced and was certainly the truth, from my point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you visit him in a group or individually? Did you go on your own or did you go with others?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: There were occasions, after I took over the CC and then the RC, where I took a team with me, but there were several occasions when I met with Mr. Kordic in my capacity as either HCC Travnik or HRC Zenica with just my interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you call announced or unannounced?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I may have visited Mr. Kordic unannounced. Usually, I made an appointment through the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see, right at the beginning of your narrative, though we didn't touch on it, about the length of his first discussion or lecture to you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I do, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about that, and tell us, if you can, not just about your assessment of him as a figure of authority but what he was like as a man.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I can't claim to know Mr. Kordic personally, but he certainly maintained the same image throughout the year that I did know him as a very, very intense political and ambitious person, very unrelenting, and I can't remember any instance where there was an advance of the peace process as a result of an initiative sponsored by Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, for example, at that first meeting, how long did he talk for uninterrupted?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: If my memory serves, the meeting went on for about two hours. Mr. Kordic gave me his version of the recent history of Middle Bosnia. Considering that it had to go through an interpreter, I believe it took about two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You'll be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Stutt. My name is Stephen Sayers. I'm one of the attorneys representing Mr. Kordic, and I'll be asking you a few questions. Just as the Prosecution told you, we speak the same language, so I would appreciate it if you could just have a short break between my question and the answer so that the interpreters can catch up. Please forgive me as I bounce around a little bit, but we did not receive the offer of proof until just a few minutes before court started, so I'll try to make it a well-organised presentation, starting out with a few general topics and then going on chronologically, much as the Prosecution did. If I ask you any questions that are not clear, just tell me. That's my fault and not yours, and it's important to get a clear record here. Now, sir, you yourself do not speak Croatian, I take it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that as a career military man, you knew virtually nothing about Balkan politics, or the politics of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the history of the country before your arrival in Zagreb towards the end of August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: "Nothing" might be too harsh a term, but I certainly did not arrive in the Balkans as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were sent, I believe, by your Department of National Defence to the former Yugoslavia in August of 1993. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And upon your arrival in Zagreb, you received what you have referred to in one of your statements to the Prosecution in 1996 as the usual briefing; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that lasted just a couple of days, I take it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How much of that briefing was actually devoted to Bosnia-Herzegovina as opposed to the rest of the countries that made up the former Yugoslavia, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Probably the bulk of the briefings dealt with Middle Bosnia, since it was the hot spot at the time. But they certainly weren't in any particularly great depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Had you studied up on Yugoslav politics or the politics and history of Bosnia-Herzegovina yourself, quite apart from the briefing that you received?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I had read two or three books prior to arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall what those were?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: "Serbs and Croats" was one, and "Another Short History of Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say that you were essentially, to coin a phrase, thrown in at the deep end in Bosnia-Herzegovina, after you had your briefing and were sent to the regional centre at Zenica?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: As often we are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to go through your duties with the European Community Monitoring Commission, Colonel. I understand that you started out initially as a monitor on team V4, with responsibility, as the Prosecution said, for Zepce, Zavidovci and Breza?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The senior team member, at that time, was Stavros Kinigopoulos, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then after a three to four weeks on the job, you then became the team leader in late September?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that you often worked alone, due to the lack of resources and personnel available to the ECMM; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then on October the 17th, you took over as the head of the coordination centre in Travnik from your predecessor Philip Watkins?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You had become the head of the coordination centre after only about six or seven weeks in the country?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And I believe, sir, that you stayed in that position until after the signature of the Washington Agreement and the conclusion of the hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Taking over as the head of the regional centre on May the 15th, 1994 from your predecessor Sir Martin Garrod?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: At the time that you became the head of the coordination centre, Travnik was actually under the control of Muslim armed forces and had been since the June offences earlier in the year that you assumed your duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were aware that the HVO had suffered significant military defeats in Travnik, Kakanj, Fojnica, Bugogno, resulting in tens of thousands of Croat refugees to other Croat enclaves. Would that be fair to say, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I am certainly aware of the general situation that was reflected on the ground when I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And after the June offences and the July offensive by the ABiH, you found the military situation confronting you, at least insofar as the Croats were concerned, was that they had been squeezed into four geographically isolated pockets: First, the Vitez-Busovaca pocket; second, the Kiseljak pocket, under the -- for all of Ivica Rajic, as you've said; third, the Zepce pocket; and finally the Vares pocket. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then the Vares pocket, of course, fell in the first week of November, resulting in, once again, a very significant wave of refugees, civilians out of Vares, Croat civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just a few questions about your perception of the chain of command in the Croat military forces, Colonel. There is no question that the headquarters of the HVO general staff was located in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe at the time that you were the head of the coordination centre in Travnik, and at all times until the end of the war the commander in chief of the HVO armed forces was General Ante Roso; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I can't remember which date he ceased being the commander, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The only point that I am making is that essentially throughout your duties as head of the coordination centre, up until the signature of the Washington Agreement, it was General Roso who was the commander in chief of the HVO armed forces; all of them, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And I believe, sir, that his chief of staff was Brigadier or by then General Milivoj Petkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: As I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to meet either General or Roso or General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, by the time that you arrived in the Vitez-Busovaca area, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna had been founded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Allegedly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And were you aware that the president of that republic was Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And as president, he was the supreme commander of the armed forces; is that right? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure if Mate Boban was a supreme commander of the armed forces or not, to be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just stepping down from the general staff level, sir. It's true, is it not, that the military organisation of the HVO armed forces was into various operative zones?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Each operative zone being commanded by a professional military man, a commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Central Bosnia operative zone, or it may have been the third operative zone by the time that you were there, was commanded by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one question with respect to General Roso, or two questions. Were you aware that he had spent over 20 years in the French Foreign Legion?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I had heard that he had served in the French Foreign Legion, as had others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And were you aware, sir, that he was not simply the commander in chief of the HVO armed forces, but that he actually sat on the nine person presidential council that was appointed on the 10th of December, 1993, that he also discharged governmental functions as well as purely military functions?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I never dealt with anything that concerned his governmental duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to Colonel Blaskic, you said in your statement, on page 3, the 1996 statement, that there was no question that he was the military operational zone commander of Central Bosnia. And that remains your view today; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe, sir, that you met with then General Blaskic after he had been promoted, after the signature of the Washington Agreement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And all of the forces in the Vitez-Busovaca pocket certainly were under the command of Colonel Blaskic during the time that you were head of the coordination centre in Travnik; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So that's the troops, special forces, military police, artillery resources, as far as you know; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And, at least organisationally, I think, it's true that the Kiseljak and Vares and Zepce pockets fell under his command; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Proceeding down from the operative zone level, it's right, isn't it, or didn't you deal at this level, but I think it's right that the operative zones were actually organised into various municipality based brigades, which reported up the chain of command to the operative zone headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the organisation, as I knew it, would ever fit in to a clean staff college line and staff presentation. But I can't argue with what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet the commander of the brigade that was based in Busovaca, the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade? I think his name was commander Dusko Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I believe I met him, but it would have been one of the team leaders that dealt with him on a regular basis. I had no personal, regular contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, we've already had the privilege of hearing from Sir Martin Garrod, and he prepared an end of tour report on April the 18th, 1994. It's already in evidence. Did you ever read that report from him?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I can't recall if I read Sir Martin's.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On page 4 of his report he says that all of the Muslim generals that he ever met were unanimously, as he puts it, hardliners. Is that your view too?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I guess that means -- I guess a definition by what you mean by hardline. In my experience, some were definitely more hardline than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever have the opportunity to meet either General Alagic or General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I met General Hadzihasanovic. I knew I dealt with General Alagic on a regular basis. And the 3 Corps replacement General Mehmed Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it that your predecessor, Sir Martin Garrod, also dealt with General Alagic and General Hadzihasanovic, as far as you know, on a fairly regular basis?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Just winding up the general questions, Colonel Stutt. Did you ever hear of a Croat political body called the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, so-called HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I may have read about it in a description or a report, but it's nothing that came up on my screen as something I had to pay attention to, doing what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, sir. And I take it from your answer that you never studied governance structure, and that you never gained an understanding of who may have been politically prominent within that organisation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I worked very hard to know who was politically prominent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: But the organisation you are describing to me isn't familiar. The community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Just on one other question. Did you know that Dr. Jadranka Prlic was the president of the civilian arm, at least of the HVO, from August the 14th, 1992, until the ministries of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna took over the governmental functions of the HZ HB and the HVO on September the 30th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Have you ever met Dr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Not that I recall, but certainly not that I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever know that he was, in fact, the president of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I would have known that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you have a contemporary understanding that there were three vice-presidents of the HVO: One, Mr. Ivankovic; one, Mr. Valenta; and the other Mr. Zubak. And you were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, we certainly knew that, but it wasn't always possible to match descriptions to personalities and power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. And did you ever have the opportunity to meet the head of the defence department, Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You made some reference during your direct testimony to the Stoltenberg Owen Plan that was approved and endorsed, I believe, by the International Community on the 6th of August 1993. It's true, sir, that the Croat contingent was the first to sign this plan, just as they had been the first to sign the Vance-Owen Plan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Stoltenberg Owen Plan actually envisaged a sort of loose federation, if you like, of three constituent republics of the three constituent peoples, Muslims, Croats and Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And were you aware that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, on paper, was founded on the 28th of August, 1993, about three weeks after the endorsement and approval of this plan by the International Community?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I don't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The founding documents, sir, and they are already in evidence, were actually signed by the chairman of the House of Representatives, a man by the name of Perica Jukic from Zepce. Did you ever have the opportunity to meet Mr. Jukic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: If he was in Zepce, I certainly did. But he was not one of the main influences in Zepce, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Zepce, if we could use a vernacular turn of phrase, was Ivo Lozancic territory, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was, in fact, the most prominent figure in Zepce and rigidly controlled the operations of affairs there, did he not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna did not have any office of vice-president?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's difficult to answer, because various reports said that there were vice-presidents, and it was very hard to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I wonder if I could just ask the usher to put this document that's previously been marked as Exhibit D143/1 onto the ELMO. This might jog your memory a little, Colonel. But if it doesn't, just tell me and we'll remove it. This is a report dated the 15th of December by the regional centre in Zenica. It's a daily report. And under paragraph 1(a), the head of the coordination centre in Mostar apparently met with a gentleman by the name of Slobodan Lovrenovic, who was the press adviser to Mate Boban. And he was explaining the functions of the recently announced presidential council, and explained that the republic, without vice-presidents, found itself in need of an alternative mechanism to support the presidential office in Boban's absence. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Does that jog your memory, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It jogs my memory, inasmuch as a report I read recently, where they referred to the possible necessity to bring a vice-president out of Middle Bosnia, but if they did that, it would have to be someone who was a quote/unquote "war hero", and that to do so would send the wrong message.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you can see, from the information that's contained shortly after the passage I just read to you from this paragraph, that Mr. Kordic didn't hold presidential office anymore but was simply an ordinary member of the house of representatives; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And, in fact, Zoran Maric, the president of the HVO in Busovaca, actually confirmed that to you in a meeting that you had with him; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: If I put it in the report, he told me that. But I guess I have to emphasise that what Mr. Kordic's actual position is -- was for a great deal or period of time, we worked very hard to determine, and the only answer we could get is that we would find out eventually, but regardless of what the position stated was, that Mr. Kordic was, in fact, the man in Middle Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel, I understand that that's your conclusion. But it would be fair to say that there was a lot of confusion surrounding Mr. Kordic's position in the really early days of this new republic that was founded on the 28th of August of '93; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It would be fair to say there was some confusion as to what the nomenclature of his position was, but there was no doubt about who you spoke to in Middle Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me address your attention to Mr. Valenta, one of the people to whom you spoke. Did you ever have the opportunity to meet him?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. He was described to you as, I believe, the vice-president of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna. This is the description that's contained on a September the 22nd, 1993, daily report which has already been introduced into evidence as Exhibit Z1211.1, vice-president of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Did you ever understand that, in fact, Mr. Valenta was never the vice-president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, I never understood that he wasn't a vice-president, but I knew that he wasn't the person I would go and speak to if I had something important to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to read Mr. Valenta's book?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just a few questions, sir, on Zepce. I believe the first visit that you made to Zepce was on September 4th, 1993. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And to get there from Vitez or Busovaca, you had to drive through territory that was controlled completely by ABiH forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, through Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, the Zenica municipality, that's right. And it would be fair to describe Zepce as a Bosnian Croat enclave that was totally surrounded by Muslim forces; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: There was a BSA back door to Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So it was surrounded by Muslims partially, and then the remainder of the circumference, if you like, of Zepce was cut off by Bosnian Serb forces; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It was not unusual to find a BSA detachment in one end of Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you talked about the Kiseljak road problems in early October of 1993, and at this point I'm going to try to pick up the pace a little bit and proceed on chronologically, just as the Prosecution did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be a convenient time, then, to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Mr. Sayers starts, I'm concerned about the timetable for today and the week, given the shortened period of time available to the Prosecution. Mr. Sayers tells me he'll go into the afternoon and take half an hour of the afternoon with this witness. I don't know if the Chamber is going to be able to -- I note that I was one hour and two minutes, I think, in chief. The number of topics covered is comparatively restrictive. I don't know if the Chamber is going to be able to sit late this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Until 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly hope we can get the other witness in and either out or nearly out today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, I don't understand what can justify, really, that you go until -- in cross-examination until this afternoon with this witness. Really, I can't understand that, because, yes, there are of course elements, but the majority of them are not very new, and I cannot understand why we have to take more time than the testimony in chief in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Two answers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: First, I'll try not to go in the afternoon, obviously. I'll try to move as quickly as I can. Second, it was extremely difficult to predict the nature of the direct examination today, because the witness covers a lot of territory. He's given very, very extensive statements, and there are a very significant quantity of documents that we had to go through. But I've made quicker progress than I thought, and I hope that I will be through by the lunch. But if I'm not, it won't be more than 10 or 15 minutes, or half an hour at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with it in the next hour and a half. That will give you two hours, twice as long as the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, you've heard we're under the gun here, so let's try to move forward smartly. Your first connection with Ivica Rajic was in early October of 1993, when apparently he was reluctant to allow UNPROFOR to improve a road between Kiseljak and Visoko, is that correct, or to repair it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct. But my contact with him was not direct; it was indirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it's true, is it not, that Colonel Blaskic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the second witness's microphone be switched on, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Am I on now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The left-hand one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Help the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Apparently, one of the microphones is not working. Let's not waste any more time, if we can. Can you speak, please, into it, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Sir, is this good?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That sounds fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's true that Colonel Blaskic had to order Ivica Rajic to repair that road; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, your -- as I understand it, sir, you talked about seven meetings with Mr. Kordic, seven that you had through your time in Central Bosnia. The first was on October the 17th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: If that's the date of my report, then that's the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And the next time that you met him was in November, and there's a report on that, as we've seen. Well, let's take it one step at a time. Mr. Kordic was essentially making political points to you regarding your conversation with him on October the 17th, 1993; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You say that Mr. Kordic was described as the vice-president of the HVO government. It's fair to say that you, yourself, did not have an understanding of the various nuances of differentiation between the HVO and the HR HB when you first met with him in October; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's fair to say, and I'm not sure I understood all the nuances when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I take your point, Colonel. You did not have a clear and precise picture in your own mind of how Mr. Kordic fitted into the political tapestry of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That would be fair to say, although I certainly understood how he fit into the power grid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me gloss over some of the points that I was going to go over with you. Let's talk about the events just before Stupni Do and the events surrounding Stupni Do, sir, since you gave a lot of testimony on that. It's true, is it not, that Vares was a geographically isolated pocket cut off from the other Croat enclaves, the Vitez-Busovaca pocket and the Kiseljak pocket being, I guess, the closest?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The civilian government of Vares consisted of Anto Pejcinovic, who was the president of the HVO government there, I believe?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: As I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Zvonko Dusnovic was the chief of military police there; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: He was military or military and civilian. I can't remember. But although you can find a list of who the important people are, it became very obvious that Zvonko Dusnovic was the person you spoke to and he influenced a degree of authority over the Bobovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the third person in authority was the chief of civilian police, Ivica Gavran?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, you met him. You did meet him, I take it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, the Muslims had established their own parallel civilian government, or war presidency as they called it, located in Dabravine to the south of Vares?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the president was Mervana Hadjimurtezic.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I've always wondered how you pronounce that, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It would be fair to say that immediately before the Stupni Do incident, there was a series of escalating incidents which caused great tension in that area. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. After the successful Muslim offensives in Travnik, Bugogno, Fojnica and Kakanj, tens of thousands refugees had left those locales, and the refugees from Kakanj, about 15.000 of them, actually relocated to Vares. Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The six soldiers that you identified who were arrested on October the 20th, sir, these soldiers were reported to you to be in uniform and carrying weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I can't recall whether or not they were carrying weapons, but they were in uniform and in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: If I so noted they were carrying weapons, then that would be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to review your statement?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your statements. All right. And you just said, on page 5 of your statement, I don't think that it's contested, that these gentlemen were supposedly carrying weapons at the time that they were apprehended.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And they were supposed to be soldiers associated with the operative group Istok or the OG East. Is that your recollection, sir, the ABiH east group?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, were you aware that the village of Kopljari had been attacked by ABiH forces on October 22, 1993, and that the entire civilian population had been displaced and all of the houses in that village burned to the ground?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I was. We were trying to find a rationale for Stupni Do. That was given as one of the theories at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In fact, in the ECMM daily summary of October the 24th, I believe it was noted, and perhaps by you, sir, it's a report that you authored. If we could just have this introduced into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document will be marked D192/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to draw your attention to the bottom of the page, sir. A United Kingdom liaison officer team, V4, learned that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had attacked and captured the Croat village of Kopljari, and you made the observation that the HVO action in Stupni Do could be in retaliation for that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That was a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You had the opportunity, I believe, Colonel Stutt, to converse with the ABiH commander in Dabravine, a man by the name of Ekrem Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he told you, I believe, that instructions had been sent by radio to the population of Stupni Do to evacuate that village on the night of October the 22nd. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And there is no question that Stupni Do was obviously in radio contact with ABiH headquarters in Dabravine at that time, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No. I'm not sure if Stupni Do was in radio contact with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But nonetheless, Mr. Mahmutovic, the ABiH commander, told you that radio contact had been established with Stupni Do the night before the attack, and that instructions to evacuate the civilian populations had been issued by the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. It was Commander Mahmutovic who actually told you that Stupni Do was a local black market gateway to BSA controlled territory; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I don't believe he was the first person to tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. In fact, a number of sources --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.
