utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- reported to you that Stupni Do was a lucrative centre for black market and smuggling in that area?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, I believe that there are a number of reports authored by the ECMM on precisely this point; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In fact, you reported, I believe, in your November the 2nd statement that has already been marked as Exhibit D117/1. I wonder if I might just put this on the ELMO so that you could have it before you, Colonel. This is an accurate copy of your report on the 2nd of November, sir, is it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It certainly appears that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And Commander Mahmutovic told you that in early October, the local HVO had demanded a substantially higher cut of the black market profits from the operations going on in Stupni Do, that this had been turned down by the Stupni Do authorities, and that the people had been killed in Stupni Do as a result of their part in the black market; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That was one of the theories put forward at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were approximately 50 members of the ABiH or Territorial Defence located in Stupni Do and that they had a variety of weapons available to them, including automatic and semi-automatic weapons and a 60-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I think in my report I counted six, so if you see six people on duty, anywhere 30 and slightly above would be accurate. If you say they had automatic and semi-automatic weapons, that certainly makes sense. I did not see a 60-millimetre mortar, but a 60-millimetre mortar is very small and easily concealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And I take it that when you visited Stupni Do, you did not ask the local soldiers to give you an inventory of all of their weapons.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Now, there's one more reference in an exhibit that's in evidence, Exhibit Z1281. I'll just read you a portion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It says that: "Hadzihasanovic told the HOM, the head of mission, that Vares was known as an area for smugglers, and gangs and groups of smugglers had been sent there to keep up tension. If the situation is tense, they can do what they want to do." Do you ever recall reading comments such as that or hearing of comments such as that from General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No. That's to say I don't recall. That's not to say there was not a statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand, Colonel. Thank you for pointing that out. Now, let's discuss Emil Harah for just a minute. Prior to the fighting in Stupni Do on October the 23rd, 1993, there's no question that he was the commander of the Bobovac Brigade in Vares; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it was Emil Harah who actually denied access to your V3 and V4 monitor teams the day after the killings in Stupni Do on October the 24th, 1993; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So it's clear that Mr. Harah was still in command of the Bobovac Brigade one day after the killings; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I am not clear precisely when Mr. Harah ceased his command. This became an issue later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Questioned by a number of sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. The only point I'm making, though, is access to Stupni Do to your V3 and V4 monitor teams was denied by Commander Harah on the 24th of October, and that's clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to the orders about which you were asked that were issued by General Petkovic, you were shown one which was a ceasefire order dated October the 24th, 1993, and that was actually sent to the commander of the Bobovac Brigade, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I had seen a copy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that's true, it was the Bobovac Brigade commander to whom that was addressed; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: To whom it was addressed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Not to any other commander in any other region, but specifically to that commander of that brigade in Vares; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The second order, sir, you weren't shown. Let me just ask the usher to put this on the ELMO for you, and I think you have seen it before. It's Exhibit Z1258, an order dated October the 23rd, 1993, issued by General Petkovic. You have, I take it, Colonel, seen this order before.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And there's no question that this order is issued to the commander of the armed forces in Vares, and it's a direction by the chief of staff of the HVO to remove three civilians from office; Anto Pejcinovic, Zvonko Duznovic and Ivica Gavran; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's correct, but you earlier described Zvonko as being the head --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Press the oblong green button, Colonel. There you go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You're quite right. But the other two gentlemen, Anto Pejcinovic and Ivica Gavran, were members of the civilian government; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Zvonko Duznovic, as far as you understood, was the chief of military police in Vares?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I thought he had a dual role.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But whatever that role was, Colonel, he was basically fired or removed from any position of authority --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- on the authority of the commander in chief of the HVO on the 23rd of October; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Sometime after October the 24th of 1993, it's clear, is it not, that Kresimir Bozic replaced Emil Harah as the commander of the Bobovac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you aware that UNPROFOR did an extensive investigation into the events at Stupni Do on October the 23rd, 1993, and that that investigation was conducted during the months following the killings of civilians in that -- and combatants in that village?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that the HVO actually attempted to do their own investigation as well by sending a colonel from Mostar, along with a military investigator, to the UNPROFOR headquarters at Kiseljak? I believe the person consulted was the head of the G1 legal section there, Lieutenant General J.W. Koet, K-O-E-T, and the individuals sent from Mostar were Colonel Vinko Lucic and Mr. Ivica Bandic. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I recall seeing a reference that an HVO investigator had made contact with UNPROFOR. No other detail beyond that, that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. There are two such reports. Let me show you one and ask you if you've seen it before, and if you have, I would like it to be introduced into evidence. If you have not seen it, then obviously we'll move on. If we put it on the ELMO, as you can see, Colonel, this is a document dated November 30th, 1993. It's entitled the first report meeting in connection with the Stupni Do incident, and it relates to a meeting that occurred on the 22nd of November of 1993, as you can see from paragraph 1, with Colonel V. Lucic, an investigator from the HVO headquarters in Mostar, Mr. I. Bandic. Have you ever seen this before?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on, then. You were aware that the NordBat had conducted interviews with about 193 persons from Stupni Do and that those interviews were transcribed and many of them were taped or videotaped; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Secretary-General of the United Nations had issued a report on February the 10th of 1994, relating to the findings of the United Nations in connection with what had happened at Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I'm aware of the report. I haven't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning to the next subject, sir, October the 25th, 1993. You said that you learned of a conversation between Sir Martin Garrod and Mr. Kordic in connection with the Stupni Do incident. It's right, isn't it, that when the subject was raised, Mr. Kordic contacted General Petkovic and asked what had happened?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And that's unsurprising for a political figure to contact the military chief of staff, if you like, to find out what had happened in a military operation; it didn't particularly surprise you to find out that he had done so? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That didn't surprise me in the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In connection with the conclusions drawn by the European Community Monitor Mission about Stupni Do, Colonel, it's true, is it not, that interviews with the evacuees from that village told representatives of your organisation that the attack had been launched by soldiers, not from the Vares area, but rather from the area of Kakanj and Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed the two units I think that you identified, one known as the Apostoli, one known as the Maturice. The Apostoli actually came or were composed of people who had fled from Travnik during the June offensive of the ABiH; is that accurate to say, so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I've heard. I'm not sure how accurate it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Maturice were composed of people who had fled from Kakanj during the June offensive as well; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe you said in your 1997 statement that all sources agreed that the killings in Stupni Do were carried out by extremist troops from Kiseljak; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It may not have been exclusively, but every report we had said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in the end-of-tour report that your predecessor prepared, and I wonder if I could just put this on the ELMO. It's already been marked as an exhibit. Thank you very much. The only part that I would like to discuss with you, sir, appears on the first page, paragraph 5. Sir Martin Garrod concluded that: "It is likely that the decision to mount the operation," and he is talking about the Stupni Do operation, "was taken at fairly low level." You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I am thinking about that. In my own mind, I'm not sure whether it was taken at a low level or not. I certainly won't interfere with anything that Sir Martin has said in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You just have a complete lack of information on that subject; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, not a complete lack of information. I'm just not certain, in my own mind, at what level the order to attack at Stupni Do was taken at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you actually went to Vares shortly after the town was captured by ABiH forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your 1996 statement you said that, by the end of October of 1993, Vares had become a military and humanitarian powder keg. I guess you still stand by that observation today, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's true that total chaos reigned immediately before the fall of Vares, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Civilian authority had basically broken down, and the military authorities were organising an imminent retreat and were, I think to use your words on page 10 of your 1996 statement, nervous to the point of panic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: They were. I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you actually saw the Bobovac Brigade headquarters gutted by fire and empty, on the 4th of November when you visited with Sir Martin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also saw the 7th Muslim Brigade members who had led the vanguard into the town, basically destroying property and looting; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I saw some of the Bobavac Brigade driving through the streets in pick-up trucks, firing into the air. The looting took place over a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Immediately following the fall of Vares, 10.000 refugees headed variously for Kiseljak and over the hills to Dastansko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, let's talk very briefly, sir, about the threat made to the UNHCR representative by Ivica Rajic. The person to whom a threat was made, I believe, was Mark DeGiulio; is that right? Or can you remember?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I can't recall the name. I wasn't at the meeting, but it was reported accurately, including the name, by the victor 3 team.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you've stated in your 1996 statement that it was reported to you that Ivica Rajic was not in command of the HVO in Kiseljak, and you knew this by the 11th of November, 1993, and had been replaced by General Petkovic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed, the Croatian press had reported that Ivica Rajic was relieved of his duties on the order of the office of the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's correct. But we've got to remember who issued the first order announcing his replacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, who did?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: In my memory, Mr. Kordic announced that at the meeting in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, sir, Mr. Kordic told you that the issue was going to be dealt with the next day; didn't he? Isn't that what your report says?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It says the issue will be dealt with the next day, in that the replacement would take place the next day. But if you talk to any of the people who were there, the representative from BiH command, the representative from UNHCR who came in from Geneva, we all left that meeting with a very clear understanding that Mr. Rajic had been replaced, the decision had been taken, and everyone could back away from the perceived crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. But you don't know who actually issued the order replacing him, do you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I only know the order I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. But you never saw a written order, did you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Not that day, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you, frankly, don't know whether this figure was removed by General Petkovic, as you said in your statement, or by someone else; do you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I know exactly who announced that Mr. Rajic was replaced, and at that moment the tension concerning the incident solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. But you did say in your statement that he was replaced by General Petkovic, and you don't know any information to the contrary?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I don't know any information to the contrary concerning General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You did say in your statement that the Croatian press had announced that this Mr. Rajic had been relieved of his duties on order of the office of the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban, and you don't know any information to the contrary of that, do you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I do believe, sir, that you never actually asked Mr. Kordic whether he had actually -- whether he actually had the power to remove people, such as Rajic, after this November the 9th meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I did not ask Mr. Kordic personally, but it was clearly understood by all of the people who attended that meeting that it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You, frankly, do not know whether Mr. Kordic has any or had any power to intervene in the military justice system that was in place in the HVO, governed as it was by rules of military discipline, and you don't know whether he -- well, let's just have an answer to that question first.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It was certainly perceived by all concerned as an intervention, but whether the order started higher, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I think that's perfectly fair, Colonel. But the fact of the matter is that you would agree that in military court martial proceedings generally, or military disciplinary proceedings generally, there really is no place for a civilian intervention, is there? Once the Prosecution is started, it runs its way through the military justice system without intervention on the part of civilians?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I wouldn't compare conventional military court martial or any other proceedings with anything I saw during my year in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand. But what I said is true? For example, in your military disciplinary system, there is no place for civilian intervention, is there, once the investigative wheels have been set in motion, so-to-speak?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I don't see the comparison, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But what I said is true, nonetheless, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: In my case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you don't know in the -- within the HVO military system whether there was any place for civilian intervention once the military wheels of justice had been set in motion, do you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it started with the military wheels of justice or the civilian wheels of justice. I maintain that the lines of command and communication were often blurred. I don't think it lends itself to a crystal clear comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But it would be fair to say, sir, that you yourself never had a discussion with Mr. Kordic about whether he had any power to intervene in the military justice system?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you never had any discussion with him, whether he had any power to issue orders, for example, to military forces, as opposed to orders coming from Colonel Blaskic or higher, General Petkovic, or General Roso; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I never questioned him about that, but I certainly understood where he fell in the power structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You discussed meetings that you had on November the 18th, 1993, with Colonel Blaskic and Pero Skopljak. Now, who was Pero Skopljak and where did he fit into the power structure, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Pero Skopljak, if I recall, and if I am wrong I'll stand corrected, was vice-president of the HDZ in Vitez. Now, if I'm wrong, I'll bow gracefully. He was a minor political figure in Vitez, and he's one of the people that you went and talked to when you were going to go out and talk to everyone. He was certainly not seen by me or my colleagues as one of the powerful figures in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were speaking to Colonel Blaskic. Would it be fair to say that Colonel Blaskic was not a politically sophisticated person; he was a military man and did not follow the political process particularly carefully?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I can't say that he didn't follow the political process carefully, but you are right in the first part of what you said, that he certainly emphasised the military dimension of his career.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask the usher to put this document on the ELMO. It's been previously marked as Exhibit D143/1, dated December the 15th, 1993. And the part to which I would like to draw your attention, Colonel, actually appears on the bottom of the page. If the usher could just move it up. Yes. There is a discussion of the HCC, whom I believe is you, meeting with Colonel Blaskic, the HVO commander of Vitez, and inquiring into the status of Mr. Kordic in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. With Colonel Blaskic explaining to you that, "I was not a politician and had not followed the political process, but they had met with Mr. Kordic earlier in the afternoon and that they were both in no doubt as to Mr. Kordic's importance in Middle Bosnia." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the military liaison officers with whom you dealt, and from whom you got information about Mr. Kordic's unclear status within the political structure, were not themselves particularly sophisticated politically, they were just regular soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's quite accurate. When we were trying to determine exactly what Mr. Kordic's actual position was, we dealt with a much wider range of people than military liaison officers. Of course, Colonel Blaskic is one of the first people we would ask, but we got the same answer, literally, from everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you said that you had developed an amicable relationship with Mr. Kordic over the year that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you felt, I think, fairly free to drop in on him whenever you wished, or to arrange an appointment to see him whenever you wished; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic always made himself available if he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. When you were having these questions in your mind around November -- October, November of 1993 about the precise status of Mr. Kordic, did you ever just sit him down and say, "Look, what exactly is your position, sir?"

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: One of the first things we wanted to do was see Mr. Kordic and ask him, and if my memory serves, Mr. Kordic was not there or available at that time, because you're quite right, that would have been one of the first things we would have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. But would it be fair to say, and I don't want to dwell on this point, but you never actually sat down with him and said, "We're in doubt, Mr. Kordic, as to what your precise position is. What is it?"

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I can't recall asking him that question, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let's move on, Colonel, and we are, I think, making progress that will allow us to finish perhaps by lunch. It's true, is it not, that the HVO was on the defensive throughout the time that you were the HCC in Travnik and that, in fact, the ABiH launched a number of offensives just before Christmas in 1993, being one of them, and then just after the new year, on January the 9th of 1994, another offensive aimed at trying to cut the main supply route just south of Santici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed this was despite a ceasefire agreement that had been reached -- the second attack was despite a ceasefire agreement that had been reached between General Rasim Delic, who had replaced General Zefer Halilovic, and General Rosso on behalf of the ABiH and HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That ceasefire did not hold.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You referred to a discussion that you had with Zoran Maric, the president of the HVO in Busovaca, sometime in December of 1993. He actually told you that Mr. Kordic's position was just one of -- one delegate in the House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I recall reading my report on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. And he was just therefore, at least at that time, December of 1993, one of 70 or so legislators in that body, in the House of Representatives; is that consistent with your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: If that's how the report went in, that's fine, but it wouldn't have attracted a particularly great deal of attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that on the 17th of February of 1994, just after, I believe, your -- just before your third meeting or fourth meeting with Mr. Kordic, he had been appointed as one of the two vice-presidents of the House of Representatives, the legislation of the HR HB?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I recall that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the president of the House of Representatives was a man by the name of Ivan Bender?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just show you one document, sir, that you were not asked about, and I believe that this document was drafted by you on the -- or is dated the 13th of July, 1994, and it basically summarises your relationship with Mr. Kordic. We'll put it on the ELMO, sir. It's a one-pager, and I have several questions in connection with it. Just so that we're all clear, this is a special report that you drafted on or about the 13th of July, 1994, and it concerns your dealings with Mr. Kordic over the preceding year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If you take a look in about the middle of the page, there's a reference to the fact that it was announced that Mr. Kordic had been appointed as assistant to the chief of staff of the HVO. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what functions, if any, he had in that position as assistant to the chief of staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, I don't. If I recall, this is after I met Mr. Kordic in Mostar, at which time he would have explained his new duties to me. But I don't know what specific duties he would have had as assistant to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. If you could just keep that report ready to hand, I have some concluding questions on that. But let me just continue through here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the number? Tell me the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number is D193/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In the meeting that you described, Colonel, with Mr. Kordic on the 16th of February, a topic of discussion arose about the newly-inaugurated and short-lived parliament of Croats in Sarajevo which Mr. Kordic expressed to you he did not regard as a legitimate institution and, in his opinion, it wouldn't stand the test of time. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The institution, in fact, sir, did not stand the test of time, did it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It kept us busy, trying to find out what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Proceeding on, sir, by this time, February the 16th, 1993, it's right, isn't it, that you understood that Mr. Boban had actually resigned as president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and that he had done so at a meeting held in Livno on the 8th of February of that year?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you know that the Presidential Council essentially took over the functions that were discharged by President Boban, with Dr. Prlic, amongst others, being on the Presidential Council?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the precise details of who took over what responsibilities exactly when Mr. Boban left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Suffice it to say, though, sir, that you do not have any information to the effect that Mr. Kordic was ever a member of the Presidential Council; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Or contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you just don't know?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Boban, however, was felt by his colleagues to have resigned for honourable reasons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I heard more than one opinion as to that, and I certainly don't know which of the opinions was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In the report, I believe, that was drafted by the regional centre in Zenica for the week of February the 13th through the 19th, 1994, the comment was made that Ivo Lozancic in Zepce bears watching because he was on the Presidential Council of the HR HB. Were you aware that the commander of Zepce was actually on the Presidential Council or were you not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I wrote that, but it wasn't because Mr. Lozancic was on the Presidential Council that I made the comment I did. I made that comment for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. There was some doubt as to who was in the political ascendancy at that point, so to speak, Mr. Kordic on the one hand and Mr. Lozancic on the other; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Some of the comments that Mr. Lozancic made to me led me to believe that he wasn't Mr. Kordic's biggest fan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm sure that's the case. And you weren't exactly Mr. Lozancic's biggest fan, were you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No. In fact, you regarded him as a little better than a hoodlum; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: He had some of those qualities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, turning to the meeting that you had with Colonel Blaskic, then General Blaskic, on April 4th of 1994, sir, he had described to you tremendous difficulties that he had in trying to exercise command over forces in the Kiseljak area; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: If we're thinking of the same report, the discussion I had with Colonel Blaskic, during that discussion he said he had difficulty exercising command and control because he had to use different techniques in each of the different areas. He didn't say it was impossible. He just said each area had to be treated differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. And, in fact, he told you that he himself had issued instructions to the chief of civil police in Busovaca to find out who may have been responsible for the destruction of the mosque in that small town in September of 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I recall the incident, not the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. But you recall that it was Colonel Blaskic who had issued instructions to the chief of civil police in Busovaca to initiate that investigation, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I don't recall that instantly, but it certainly sounds logical, and I'm not going to question it if you have it in one of my reports. It doesn't leap to memory, but it sounds reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me see if I can jog your memory. In the statement you gave to the prosecutors over the course of about a week in July of 1996, June and July, on page 17 you said that Colonel Blaskic introduced the chief of civil police and said his instructions were to find out the persons responsible for the destruction of the mosque in Busovaca and frame charges; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in all the time that you knew Colonel Blaskic and met with him, he never contended at any time that he was in any way somehow subordinated to Mr. Kordic and had to take military orders from Mr. Kordic, did he, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, he didn't, but on a couple of occasions he reminded me, as is in one of the reports, that everybody understands what Mr. Kordic's position in Middle Bosnia is, which is a neither/nor answer, in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But the point is he never insisted to you that Mr. Kordic had any kind of individual unilateral authority to issue orders to the military outside of the normal chain of command, did he?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: He never said that, but he never said he didn't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And when you met Brigadier General Blaskic at that point, he was the second in command to General Petkovic in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Podgorica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Podgorica, yes, I'm sorry. Wherever it was, but the point I'm making is that he was the second in command to the commander in chief of the entire HVO; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And his replacement as commanding officer of all of the HVO forces in Central Bosnia was now General Filip Filipovic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Indeed, sir, you had some discussions with Brigadier General Blaskic concerning the extremist gangs in Kiseljak, and I believe that Brigadier General Blaskic instructed you that the identity of the wrongdoers and perpetrators of criminal acts was known and that they would be dealt with in due course; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, you yourself noticed, over the course of your duties as head of the coordination centre in Travnik, that there was, over the course of October of 1997 to the signature of the Washington Agreement, a gradual increase in the efficiency of the Croat police and that there was a reduction in the amount of crime that was actually going on in your area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: After the Washington Agreement and the cessation of hostilities, things became easier to do everywhere. However, in despite of that, there were still continuous reports of gang activity, particularly in Kiseljak and Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. But the point that I'm making is that Brigadier General Blaskic at that point told you that the identity of the wrongdoers was known and that --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I recall him telling me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, turning to a meeting that you described in your direct examination on May the 20th, 1994, with Mr. Kordic, you said that you were surprised at this meeting by the reasonable and moderate attitudes and statements that he made about the agreed cantons in the new Federation government and that you ascribed this to having been read the riot act by President Tudjman, the president of Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Kordic was one of about 100 or so people who were part of the delegation from Central Bosnia visiting Zagreb and President Tudjman between February 1994 and May of 1994?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I wasn't able to count them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know how many people actually were part of that delegation --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. You are not suggesting that this was an individual mission, if you like, by Mr. Kordic to President Tudjman in Zagreb, and that there was a one-on-one meeting at which he was specifically individually read the riot act, as you put it? You just don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I don't know if there was a one on one. But I accurately reported a change in attitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely. But the change in attitude was not just on the part of Mr. Kordic, it was on the part of the other HVO politicians in the area as well, wasn't it? And you did notice that change in attitude?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: The change in attitude in some of the other places happened a little bit sooner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You referred to a conversation that you had with Mr. Kordic some time in the middle of 1994, when he confided to you that he had been appointed to the rank of brigadier in the reserves of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he told you that this was a largely ceremonial function, and in fact you actually recorded that in your July the 13, 1994 report, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: His future was with the HDZ, and he planned to be involved in Cantonall politics from that time forward, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that he had actually been a vice-president of the HDZ, BiH political party from November the 14th, 1992, continuously, until he actually became the president of that party in July of 1994?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, I certainly didn't know that, because it was a long -- a wide period of time where no one could tell us precisely what his official position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Two final subjects. HV troops. It's true that one of the reasons the ECMM presence was established first in Central Bosnia was to monitor the alleged presence of HV troops there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you yourself never saw any HV troops during the entire year that you spent in Central Bosnia, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I didn't, but I got reports from some of the teams who did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you are not personally aware of any HV armed forces from the Republic of Croatia ever being involved in combat in any of the pockets of Croats in Central Bosnia? By that I mean the ones that I've just identified, Vitez, Busovaca --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, not in the pockets, but their presence was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to finish up my cross-examination. I would just like to ask you a few concluding questions on your July the 13th, 1994 report, Colonel. You made the observation that Mr. Kordic was the only senior Croat politician who looked beyond the immediate conflict with the Muslims to the future; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To more distant political and military objectives, I think as you put it? In fact, he told you that one of his responsibilities was to look ten years into the future, to try to envisage what life would be like in Central Bosnia ten years in the future; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Kordic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, indeed, you made the observation that in your discussions with him he appeared frequently not to be aware of many of the nitty-gritty joint commission issues of the moment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: He was always aware of the wide policy issues, but he was not aware of 12-figured grid references.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I mean, he was a big picture political figure and he didn't concentrate on the nitty-gritty of operational matters, either in a detailed --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Not to the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you made the observation in your report that Mr. Kordic had a reputation as being an extremist, but you say that that was not precisely correct. And you are still of that view; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Well, I guess what do we mean by extremist? From the time I first met Mr. Kordic throughout, he was always hard and unrelenting and probably the last person to exercise a flexible option on a peace process. When I said he wasn't an extremist, he always spoke very eloquently, and wasn't given to completely irrelevant statements that you would attribute to an extremist of a different sort. He is certainly an extreme man, but he argued his case very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. I mean, he never made racially derogatory remarks about Muslims to you in your presence, did he?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I don't recall Mr. Kordic ever making a racial slur against the Muslims, but he certainly didn't have much time for the BiH or the people in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. But you would have to agree, sir, that having been a leading political figure during the preceding year, there had been a lot of --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic did not make racial slurs in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And finally you said that Mr. Kordic was distrustful of Muslims. But that's not an unreasonable position to adopt, in your view, given the fact that there had been a civil war going on for about a year; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That was right up until we had the cessation of the hostilities and the Washington Agreement, and after that, frankly, most of us were amazed by how much trust got pulled out of the hat in a sincere effort to make things work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And you said that in your report that Mr. Kordic was distrustful of Muslims, but it is wrong to grant him as an extremist, which has a perpetrator of radical acts connotation. And that's still your view today, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one final question in this regard. There is no question that after the Stupni Do incident, Mr. Kordic was one of the first persons to condemn any kind of atrocities anywhere, regardless by whom they were perpetrated; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Everybody condemned it, and it was a contest to see who could be first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. But Mr. Kordic also condemned it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: As one of the many.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Colonel, thank you very much indeed. That concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. We will not have cross of this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few other questions, Colonel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about whether the forces were under Blaskic's control. In your judgement, where, if at all, did Blaskic and his decision-making fit into a political structure?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I don't think any of us were absolutely certain who was entitled to give orders and who wasn't entitled to give orders. The chain of command did not match a staff college line and staff diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it had matched a staff college plan, where does the politician fit in, in relation to military command?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Fall in. In most countries politicians establish the policy and the military carries it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about Sir Martin Garrod's end-of-tour report. It wasn't shown to you in detail, but there was a suggestion about the Muslim commanders being hardline. What Sir Martin actually said was, in relation to Hadzihasanovic and Pasalic, commander of the 4th BiH Corps handing over to Bukdakovic [phoen], he said this: That Hadzihasanovic's promotion was of interest, as he had been hardline, as indeed had Alagic in his determination to achieve a united Bosnia. In the same report Sir Martin said this, at page 4: Of the Croat side, he said that they were not, certainly in the first part of the period in question, interested in a united Bosnia and wanted their own state within it. So that's the way in which the term "hardline" is used --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm afraid I must object. What I had in mind was paragraph 26 of Exhibit 119-1, which says: All the BiH generals with whom I came into contact on a regular basis were unanimously hardline, determined to fight on either for a united Bosnia or for their territorial demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, the use of the united Bosnia. Do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you are going to have to ask me again what I am agreeing to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He's twice referred to their hardline approach in relation to having a united Bosnia, not a segregated Bosnia. And once he refers to there being possibly hardline in relation to their own territorial aims. Do you agree with him in relation to their being "hardline" in relation to their wanting a united Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I agree that they were hardline to continue their existence. I'm not sure how long -- how hardline they were personally about a united Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other half of that summary that I read out was the reference to the desire of the Croats, at least initially, to have their own state within Bosnia. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of the documents, I think it's 1258, but we needn't look at it again, was the three removals from office allegedly taking effect on the 23rd of October. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any reason to accept the dating of those removals as genuine; any external evidence coming to you to show that that was correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about Kordic contacting Petkovic in relation to what happened at Stupni Do. Does his contacting a high-level military person fit or otherwise with your general view about his position in Central Bosnia and his power there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: It's completely in concert with my personal opinion as to his power in Middle Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One matter of detail. You were asked about looting by the 7th Muslim Brigade and you gave an answer that dealt with shooting in the air by the Bobovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, no. Shooting in the air by the 7th Muslim Brigade. The looting took place over about a two-week period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case I think the transcript may have misgot it, or you may have misplaced a word. So what you were speaking of was shooting in the air by the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. At the meeting with Kordic about Rajic, was there any suggestion by him, or anyone else, that he had to refer the decision about Rajic elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked several questions about who actually removed Rajic. Once the decision had been made to remove the man, do you know, one way or another, whether he would have had to be technically removed by a military or a civilian person?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No, I don't know, but the order given on that day was seen and understood by all of the attendees at the meeting to be the executive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there ever any need to ask Kordic what his powers were? If not, why not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Possibly because -- although we were certainly very interested in finding out what his specific position on paper was, those of us who dealt with Mr. Kordic on a regular basis had no doubt how important he was. Sometimes it's embarrassing to ask somebody what he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been suggested to you today that he was a big picture political figure, but I don't think any particular role has been suggested, just a big picture political figure. From the cross-examination you've had today, does the picture of Mr. Kordic become any clearer to you, or are you left in the same position as you were in 1993 and 4?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I've certainly learned some blackened detail I didn't know before, but other than that I stand by the reporting I did a number of years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does your opinion on his power and authority remain?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Exactly as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked whether you had an amicable relationship with him, and you answered affirmatively to that. But just explore that a little bit more. Amicable might suggest friendship, or it might suggest a relationship characterised by aspects of humanity and so on. Just tell us --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Kordic and I ever delved much into the way of humanitarian issues on a personal level. We didn't discuss much on a personal level. Amicable is exactly what the meaning of the word is, I think. We were always polite to each other. I think we treated each other with respect, and there was never any tension between the two of us personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any affection ever developed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I don't think so. No, I think is the honest answer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any reason or event that occurred to lead you to believe that there was an independent HVO court martial system?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been shown the document D193.1. It's unfortunate that it wasn't shown to you by us. It slipped through the net of retrieved documents, so you haven't had a chance to review it. You've still got it in front of you, and just remind yourself --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I have it and I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've been taken through various parts of it. In the middle it says, and somebody's underlined it, maybe the original underlinings, that the HVO would only ever fight with the BiH when it was in the Croat's interest to do so, and would never assist with purely Muslim military interests. And then you turn to the change in attitude from Zagreb. You then say that he -- you asked him about this, and he smiled and said there was a different mood now, and went on to deal with becoming a brigadier. Anything else on that that you can remember, or does it speak for itself?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I think it's clear. I'm happy to answer any questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally just two other questions of Stupni Do. You've told us about -- in detail, you've told us the numbers and the equipment that they had by way of defence when you visited them. How clear or otherwise was your impression then, is your impression now, of what was the nature of the defence, if any, going on at Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: There was no apparent defence system internally within Stupni Do. It bore none of the signs of stress that you would see in other areas, nor did it have any of the signature of caches of ammunition or large-calibre weapons, which usually leave a trail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you were asked a question about Mr. Kordic's power to issue military orders. What view were you able to form about his power to either issue military orders or to influence them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: I always saw and understood Mr. Kordic to be the senior Croat in Middle Bosnia, regardless of whether he was wearing a uniform or not, and personally I doubt if anything substantial was ever decided without his having a major input into that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about the level of decision making at Stupni Do, and you declined to be drawn on whether it was a low-level or middle-level or high-level decision. Does that remain your position?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: That remains my position. It's very easy at the time to put a comment in a report, and that wasn't my comment either, and in my own mind, and I certainly thought about it often enough, I don't know whether it was a low- or high-level decision to do what happened in Stupni Do. I always wondered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we saw -- sorry. We saw that the comment about it being a low-level decision wasn't premised by but I think was followed by a reference to the black market explanation. The black market explanation was one of several, I think.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: Yes, two or three I can think of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So when you said it's easy to put a comment in a report, forget the instant comment about Stupni Do, but when you're trying to build a picture of an event, you obviously look at the then existing other material. In this case, I think Sir Martin was obviously looking at the evidence about the black market.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM STUTT
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. That's all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you very much for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. Your evidence is now concluded. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Scott is taking the next witness. He was told, because of what we understood, that it was going to be after lunch. I believe the exhibits may not be in a final position. Would it inconvenience the Chamber to take an early lunch or would you like me to summon him down and get him started, come what may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Early lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And one administrative matter while the witness is withdrawing. The Chamber will recall a short discussion last week about affidavits, about the fact that the statements to which the affidavits related had been served a long time before, about the fact that there is a seven-day rule built into the procedure which may be abbreviated, and about the fact that in respect of two of the statements, there had been some amendments made before the judge in Bosnia. On Friday afternoon, we served -- or maybe Friday evening, we served the Defence with draft translations of the amendments made by the two witnesses. I see Mr. Sayers shaking his head. I've seen the letter this morning which sent it out, so it may have been a slip-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just so the position is clear, Mr. President, we were delivered the Croatian versions of the so-called affidavits at the close of business last Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course they were. What I'm concerned with is the amendments, if any, and they were served, I think, last Friday by letter, so that although they don't have the nuts and bolts of the formalities of the affidavit in translation, they have got all the material information in translation as of last Friday, and of course the affidavits themselves are served in a language that the accused themselves, and in each case lawyers on one side and on both sides, understand. So I'm going to be asking in due course for an abbreviation of the time period so we can resolve the affidavit issue, and I would ask that there be an abbreviated so that we can deal with it on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only authority, as I understand it, for affidavits under 94 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, what is the prejudice to you if we do abbreviate the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's no prejudice, Mr. President. That's not the point that I was going to make. The point is that Rule 94 ter specifically provides that affidavits on specific facts can only corroborate the testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a different point. The point that's made at the moment is to ask for an abbreviated time, which we're minded to give, and we'll hear the matter on Wednesday. And then, of course, you can make your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. 2.15, please. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m. 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If it please the Court, Colonel, your full name is Lieutenant-Colonel Remi Landry in the Canadian Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You graduated from the Royal Military College in Montreal, Canada, and received a Master's Degree in Political Science from the University of Montreal in 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You have been a professional, and still are, if that's correct, a professional infantry officer, a parachutist, or paratrooper, and a chief instructor at the Canadian Infantry Training School; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You are currently employed at the International Peace Academy in New York; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in the course of your professional military career you have received Canada's Order of Military Merit?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that at about the end of February, 1993, you became a member of something called the European Community Monitoring Mission or ECMM?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You spent your tour with ECMM in Central Bosnia primarily at the regional centre called RC Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During your time you were also involved in the Busovaca Joint Commission. You thereafter held a number of positions in ECMM for the remainder of your tour, including chief of operations and deputy chief of mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct. All that took place within the RC Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And your tour in Bosnia continued until about late August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you describe, please, to the Court, Colonel, in ECMM's view, of what you saw in the first half of 1993 of anything such as a strategy or plan on behalf of the Bosnian Croats in connection with territory or municipalities or Cantons in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just interpose a preliminary objection, Your Honour. In the offer of proof here that we received at 2.00 today, it looks like the witness is going to propose to express a lot of political opinions here, as opposed to military opinions, to which we would not object. We do object to all of the political subjective opinions that apparently the witness is going to be asked to utter, as beyond the scope of his competence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, if you could stay within the witness's expertise on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour, although we would consider that expertise, Your Honour, be consistent with other senior officials of ECMM, who had both and expressed opinions on both military and political matters, as came up during the course of their professional duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, in the first half of 1993, did you see any plan or strategy on behalf of the Bosnian Croat leadership to implement some interpretation or view of the Vance Owen Peace Plan, and if so, can you describe that briefly to the Court?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I would say that after a month upon my arrival, it became obvious that the HVO were having a double standard practice on the ground. I mean by that, that whatever troop was in Central Bosnia or south of Central Bosnia, they appeared to fully cooperate with the Bosniak Muslim forces, while the same troops wearing the same uniform to the north of Central Bosnia, and here I refer to Tuzla, were more or less living in harmony and cooperating fully with the Muslim Bosnian. And then it became apparent that through other contact with UNPROFOR, other contact within Zagreb, that there was some kind of tacit understanding that was being talked within all those organisation; that they heard that probably there was a kind of plan, master plan between Croatia and between Serbia that, in fact, they were going to split Bosnia in two parts, and Central Bosnia and the southern part of Bosnia was eventually to go to Croatia. And the northern part of Bosnia was to go to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was your understanding of how that plan, as you've just described it, related to the Vance-Owen Plan as put forth by the International Community?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, this is precisely the point of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's not giving a political opinion. He was on the ground at the time. Now, Colonel, I'm sure you can deal with this fairly briefly. What was your understanding of the position?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: As soon as the plan was announced to have been signed between the Bosniak Muslim and the Bosniak Croat at the end of March, it became very, very, very apparent that the HVO in Central Bosnia and in the southern part of Bosnia wanted to implement the plan as quickly as possible. But again it was our perception, and when I say "our", I mean the staff of the ECMM mainly in Zenica, that the plan was to be -- or at least the Vance-Owen Plan was to be implemented according to the perceptions of the HVO, which, for example, called for encouraging Muslim inhabitants basically in Central Bosnia to quit, to leave the village that they were living in, and eventually accommodate Croats that were, for example, living in Zenica and offering them to return to Central Bosnia or at least the parts which would belong to the provinces that would be under the control of the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Is it accurate to say, Colonel, that in the first part of 1993, it was ECMM's assessment that the HVO at that time was in a strategically-stronger position in relation to or in comparison to the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it was our assessment, and it could be easily seen on the ground. It's no surprise for us to realise that the Bosnian Muslims were fighting basically on two fronts and instead of sharing the same aim or the same goals with the Croats in Central Bosnia while they were facing a force which was not cooperating at all, which was attempting by all means to delay or to keep adding -- how should I say -- to keep adding elements to an already-agreed ceasefire, and that's what we could see throughout the first months that I was there, February and March. And as we were closing up to the mid-April, we could even see a further deterioration of the overall situation. As you must recall, the Busovaca Joint Commission was there to implement the ceasefire agreement that had already been signed earlier on that year throughout Central Bosnia, and the commission was eventually to see that both sides were cooperating to implement the ceasefire. And one side, on numerous occasions and repeatedly, were attempting to delay the implementation of this ceasefire, knowing very well that the Muslims were in a very difficult situation and would eventually accept the addition of those new -- of those added elements to the ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's be clear about this, Colonel. When you say "one side would engage in a series of delays," which side are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Talking about the HVO, the Bosniak Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And also just to be clear, when you said a few moments ago that the Muslims were fighting on two sides or on two fronts, which fronts were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, I was talking the front that the Serbs -- I mean the Bosniaks were fighting the Serbs to the north and slightly to the north-west of Central Bosnia, and as this was taking place, they were fighting through the south part of Central Bosnia, Jablanica and all that. They were under a lot of fighting in the Fojnica area, and this was taking place basically against the HVO forces, and this was taking place while they were attempting to implement this ceasefire agreement in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you see about the approach that the Bosnian Croats took to the plan that was different or in contrast to the plan as you understood it to be properly implemented or intended by the International Community? I want you to be very specific in terms of any specific differences you saw between what you understood and what ECMM understood the plan for the provinces or cantons to be and what you saw the Bosnian Croats doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: As I basically said earlier, as soon as the plan was agreed by HVO and then eventually by the Bosniak Muslims, the interpretation of exactly how this plan should be implemented seems to be slightly different from the point of view of the actual Vance-Owen Plan. I must say here, Your Honours, that RC Zenica, as soon as the plan was accepted, received a task to facilitate the implementation of this plan, and that's why most of the monitors became very knowledgeable about this plan. The plan agreed that, yes, three provinces were to become Croat, three provinces were to become basically majority of Bosniak Muslim, three Serbs, and one was -- Sarajevo was to be some kind of the three ethnic provinces. But in each of those provinces, the leadership of the provinces was supposed to be headed by the minority that had -- the majority -- had the majority within those provinces, but it was very clear to us that this was supposed to be done with the tolerance of the other minorities and that sometimes the Vance-Owen Plan did say that some of the governing or some of the representative positions had to be sure with the majority and with the minority. And in addition to that, all parties that did sign this agreement were to allow free traffic so that, in fact, basically the central provinces, which were Muslim, were to have access to a line of communication to be able to resupply and all that, and all we could see during the month of April was that it seems that the Croats -- the HVO had a different interpretation of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to -- and especially for the benefit of the interpreters, if you could speak just a bit more slowly, Colonel. Also, let me hand you or ask the usher, please, to hand you two exhibits to begin with, or actually one is a -- the first is 394.1, and then there's also a bundle, if you will, of exhibits starting with 571.3. If those could be distributed, please. It might be helpful, usher, if we could please put a copy of 394.1 on the ELMO. Now, starting with 394.1 -- excuse me a moment. We can step back in time for a moment. Looking at this document, do you recognise the format and content of this document to be the type of ECMM report that you, from February to August of 1993, became very familiar with, and in fact, I'm sure, authored a number of reports such as this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the record, this is a report dated the 25th of January, 1993, titled "Fightings between Muslims and Croats in Central Bosnia," a special report. If I can direct your attention down to the end of what is paragraph numbered 2, where it says: "What is at stake there is not a local problem (the two local commanders did not look very much like enemies) but certainly a political purpose close to ethnic cleansing." And item 3: "The dangers for the whole area are obvious, for the outcome of the Geneva talks, for the fate of the populations, as well as for the possible interference of Islamist forces encouraged by the victimisation of the Muslim community." When you got on the ground in Central Bosnia in February, did ECMM understand, and did you come to understand that the concept of the different groups or ethnic factions, having different claims on territory, or competing with each other for territory was already an issue?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. It takes -- it took maybe a week or so, and then I was being able to benefit from the expertise of my colleague. And eventually, since I was directly involved with the Busovaca Joint Commission, then I came to have quite a thorough understanding of what was going on, and what was a real issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the first sub item under paragraph 3. Even as of January of 1993, is it fair to say, Colonel, that the future of the Muslim or BiH troops in the Croat-held provinces was one of the issues or concerns?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me then ask you to go to Exhibit 571.3, which, Mr. President, is the first document in a bundle of documents. And these particular documents, we have compiled a set in the order in which they will be presented to the witness for, hopefully, ease of reference. I think there will be no dispute, Your Honour, that this exhibit, or part of it at least, is part of the Vance-Owen Plan, as signed by some of the parties toward the end of March of 1993. Colonel, I would like it direct your attention to page number 5 of annex 4. Or if one is to use the handwritten numbers that have been placed in the upper right corner, it would be page 7 out of 22. I am going to direct your attention to the first numbered paragraph 1 on the bottom of that page. If you could just look at that and give the Court a moment to look at --

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Did you say paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Paragraph numbered 1 on the bottom of that page, under the heading "Interim Provincial Governments." Having this document in front of us, Colonel, is it fair to say that this reflects or indicates what you were testifying about a few minutes ago, that the concept of the Vance-Owen Plan and the cantons or provinces were that there -- where there would be a majority population, there would still be a proportional representative system of government?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at the bottom of that page, it indicates: "On the basis of the composition of the population of the province based on the results of the 1991 census."

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you take it from that, then -- well, not really just you personally, but ECMM have the understanding that the fact that a particular province might be referred to as a "Croat" province, did not mean that it would be -- that the powers to be or the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I don't think we need go into all of this. We've had evidence about it, and it will be a matter of interpretation for us. We've been over this -- just one moment. Time is limited this week. We are under much pressure. And I see there are at least another six witnesses to be done in the next two days. So I must ask you to complete your examination-in-chief in the next hour, in order to allow the Defence to cross-examine, and in order to get on with our business.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
