utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. We'll do everything we possibly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just finish by simply pointing that paragraph out. And I don't think these particular paragraphs, Your Honour, have ever been specifically put before the Court. If I can just point out one other paragraph and then move on. I would direct the Court and with the witness, only to the extent the Court may have a question, to page -- let me again use the pages on the top right corner, 9 of 22. The section indicated "Withdrawal of Forces." And just by way of pointing out to the Court, Your Honour, if the Court will allow me one question. On the bottom of that page, Colonel, the second -- excuse me, the third full sentence of that paragraph provides, does it not, "Both Bosnian army and HVO forces shall be deployed in provinces 5, 8, 9 and 10, under arrangements agreed between them." Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again the concept was not that the HVO would be the only military force in a "Croat" province; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is our understanding. Yes, it is my understanding, and was the understanding of ECMM at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Court will just give me one moment, I'll try to edit down as I go here. If I could summarise a couple of the points or questions together, if the Court will allow me. Colonel, can you tell the Court whether it was -- it appeared to you, and to ECMM, that the Bosnian Croats, in carrying out, or their view of the Vance-Owen Plan, did you see or observe that they seemed to be going on two tracks or two levels at the same time? Can you describe that to the Court, briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Okay. When you refer to two levels, I gather that you must refer to the fact that since we were working on the ground with the local commander, it seems that those local commanders were to -- eventually to agree to the ceasefire, were eventually able to show signs of compliance to the plan and to the ceasefire, and eventually to this acceptance of the Vance-Owen Plan. And at the same time, it seems at the very higher level, the political level of the HVO, it seemed that they were never satisfied with what was taking place on the ground, and seems that they were trying to get something more from the Bosniak. They were never satisfied with the plan as it was. They wanted to -- my gathering is that they wanted to have the full control of those Croat provinces and have the full control of the forces that were within those provinces. And at the same times we were attempting to get to them to agree to have a joint headquarters, where again we felt that this was -- this was the -- what the Vance-Owen Plan, by having a kind of cohabitation of both forces in either Croat majority or Muslim majority provinces. And yet, even though we saw evidence that later on in April and early May that this joint headquarters was put together, it was never given the resources, the strength and the authority to do what it was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Court will allow me to combine about four or five questions together. Did you see, Colonel, that on the one hand there was a level at which the HVO would present itself to the International Community as conciliatory and anxious to accomplish a true peace agreement in Bosnia, but did you see a different set of events or acts on the ground?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: To be very brief, and to repeat what I said, yes. In fact, that if my memory is correct, they were the first ones to sign the Vance-Owen Plan. And yet, at the same time, this attitude was not really put forward and we could not really feel that that's exactly what was their intention. Their intention seems to be to try to get the kind of international support and eventually head up doing something else on the ground, which was not really within the spirit of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to point the Court to two exhibits and simply note them now, to move on, in the interests of the Court's guidance and time. If I could direct the Court to Exhibit 595 in the bundle and 595.1. Let me just represent to the Court, Exhibit 595, the record and the evidence would show, Your Honours, is a proposed joint statement by Mate Boban, purporting to be an implementation of at least certain parts of the Vance-Owen Plan. I would simply point the Court, for the present purposes, to paragraph 4, indicating a supposed deadline by the 15th of April, 1993. I would also then, in Exhibit 595, Your Honour, point the Court to a document tendered to another Trial Chamber previously, a communication from President Alija Izetbegovic from Bosnia, dated the 22nd of July, 1997, in which President Izetbegovic indicated that he, in fact, never signed the joint statement with Mate Boban. That is Exhibit 595.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to realise during this time, and by "this time", I'm now at the end of March and into April of 1993, after the Vance-Owen Plan was signed, that -- did it come to your attention that the Bosnian Croat side was increasingly frustrated or concerned, if you will, with what they saw as lack of cooperation with the implementation of the plan, of the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I think that it was well sure again within my colleagues that even though things seem to be going ahead at the local level, that there was a lot of frustration, a lot of tension in the air. And it seems that other incidents were popping up in Central Bosnia, in the Lasva Valley, that were indicative of something else. I was, for example, very optimistic that we were going to be able to accomplish the filling up of the trench in a certain area of Central Bosnia, and yet at the same time we had all those indications that other incidents involving ethnic hate involving violence that were popping up in different locations were indicative that something wrong was going on. But we could not exactly put our finger on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, please, to Exhibit Z639.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just inquire whether these documents have previously been provided to us pursuant to the timetabling order? I must say this particular document does not look familiar, although, of course, it is possible that it has been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think this particular document has, Your Honour, because Mr. Landry produced it to us yesterday. Or it was our understanding that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's see what the document is. I'm not sure. Is it in this bundle, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I guess it isn't, Your Honour. That's what I -- it is? I'm not sure, Your Honour. I thought it was, but it may have been -- I'm sorry. If the usher can -- it's 639.1, Your Honour. I don't know what's happened. Mine are in order. I don't know where they are now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. What is the point on here that you want the witness to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point -- first of all, I would ask the witness to identify the document as being an ECMM document, and this particular one concerning the Canadian contingent, similar, Your Honour, excuse me, to reports -- the type of reports up the ECMM chain of command, as the Court has seen before, this one dated the 11th of April, five days, for instance, before Ahmici. And I direct the Court's attention to page 5 of 9, the top of that page, which I think is directly relevant to the line of testimony we've been pursuing for the last few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just as a matter of principle, Your Honour, and in two seconds, the Court's timetabling order of the 21st of January, 2000, required all exhibits to be delivered to us by the 28th of January, and here, as in previous cases, we see yet more exhibits popping up. And so I object on the grounds of untimely delivery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you know, no doubt the witness, of course, trying to assist, brought this document with him, and it may be you've admitted it for the same reason. But there has to be a limit to the number of documents that we have. I myself am currently reviewing your outstanding exhibits, which are hundreds of exhibits long. For that reason, we're not going to admit another one. The point is one that has been covered elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just -- I think it's been the Prosecutor's understanding, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it is not a matter for argument, Mr. Scott. We've ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If we could then authenticate then, before moving on, several exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher to hand you Exhibit 852.4, 890.1, and 972. If you can just look at those, the only questions for the present purposes, Colonel, are looking at these documents, are these all documents that you obtained or received in the course of your tour of duty with ECMM in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, for instance, on 852.4 and 890.1, it indicates, in fact, that these particular documents were faxed between two different components of ECMM; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on Exhibit 972 -- just for point of reference, Your Honour, I'm looking a little below the middle of the page for Province number 10, indicating Mr. Kordic to be a member of the provincial government of Province number 10. Colonel, did you receive this particular document in the course of, again, your duties with ECMM, and why was it that ECMM would be interested in this particular information?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: As I've mentioned to you, we -- earlier, we were given the task by ECMM headquarters to facilitate the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, so naturally all this information was crucial to help us out to eventually facilitate the process to create those provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And concerning Province number 10, among those being nominated for positions in that provincial government included Mr. Valenta, Mr. Skopljak, and again Mr. Kordic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward, then, beyond the other exhibits in the outline for present purposes, did you -- can you describe to the Court what role, if any, from a policy perspective, did ethnic division play, if it did, in the HVO programme that you saw being carried out?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, most of the work that we were doing within the Busovaca Joint Commission was basically to, as I was saying earlier, to implement a ceasefire, but most of the work that we had to deal with, basically complaint and protests that minority ethnics were suffering from the majority ethnics which were around. And I must say that starting basically in April, a lot of those minority ethnics appear to be Muslim, were Muslim living basically in Central Bosnia. And I can recall, for example, the work that they did in Skradno, which is a small village or very close to Busovaca, where we had to go there on a regular basis because people were eventually confined to stay within the village and were -- all type of pressures were being exercised on them to force them to quit. True --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say "quit", what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: To leave the premises of the small village so that, in fact, they could vacate their house and eventually the house be given to somebody else that was of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your observation on the ground, Colonel, did you see that -- by and large, did you experience that the ethnic division was something that was experienced, if you will, at the grassroots level, or from the bottom up, or was it a policy from the top down?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I would tend to believe again that it was a policy from the top down, because there is numerous incidents, and if the Court wants to know more about that, I can provide examples where it appears to us that there was, in fact, much more harmony between the ethnics than appears to be when looked from the outside, and it seems that when we were gaining this type of -- when we were able to achieve reconciliation -- local reconciliation, not too long after again there was incidents that were awakening again, revenge, and it was very difficult for us to be successful because we just felt that the higher authorities in charge, be it either the military or the political authority, okay, were not supporting what, in fact, we had been asked to help them out to implement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just a couple of specific stories, Your Honour, by the witness, but we'll pass through those -- over those in the outline.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You mentioned Skradno a few moments ago, Colonel. Did you -- is that one of the places where you saw efforts by the HVO, by various tactics, to move the Muslims out of that community?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Exactly. You must realise that as the commission was sitting in the morning, what we used to do is that in the afternoon we were investigating the protests that were being presented to us, and Skradno happened to be one of the first protests that I was personally involved with. And I kept involved for at least two months by paying visits on a regular basis to the people -- inhabitants of Skradno.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What I want you to do now, just very briefly Colonel, just go very specifically to a particular practice where the Muslims may have been lined up and shot at in some fashion. If you'd just describe that very briefly to the Court.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: The first incident, what's very close to my memory, is as I was -- as I entered this village, there was a woman that came running at me, crying, asking protection. And then I found out later on, through our interpreter, that she and the rest of her family had been put into the motion of every night, as the darkness was falling on the village, people dressed up in black were knocking at her door, and then were more or less lining up all the inhabitants. Her husband was not there. And then they were lining up all the inhabitants of that house on the outside wall and then were just going through the motion of an execution party, by firing their weapon. Naturally, I was able to see all the holes above the heads of the people that were still there on our own. And again the idea was to force them to leave the village. And as they were about to do it, well, they had to sign a paper saying that they were leaving the village on their true will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's probably clear, but when you say they were lined up and shot at, intentionally they were shot over -- the shots were fired over their head?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, over their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then they were told that they could leave the village if they signed a paper saying they were doing so voluntarily and would not come back?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: But again you have to understand that that was not what was taking place. I mean, they were not offering right away to leave the village. It's just the next day, for example, if they wanted to quit the village, since the village was being always guarded by civilian police, they were then told, "Well, if you quit, you will have to sign this paper, and you will not be allowed to come back." And another incident was stealing their car, stealing their farming equipment, not allowing them to go and to harvest their field, that type of incident was taking place on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Colonel, we are going to have to move forward. I am going to direct your attention to early April of 1993. Was there a particular turn of events in Travnik about that time, in terms of the dealings between the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, I must tell you that the second week of Travnik, and the rest of the month of April was very, very busy and very intense. There were all kinds of activities and all kinds of conflict and all kinds of violence that took place. It started with -- the whole story started basically with the raising of Croatian flag in Travnik. And that more or less generated frustration from the part of the Muslims. It was then followed by HVO officers that were being kidnapped. Then Muslims that were being -- soldiers that were being killed in Travnik, then some of the elected Muslims within the city of Travnik were ousted out because it didn't make any sense to have the capital of these provinces, and to have at the head of the city, while no Muslim people. And then all that generated into quite a very increase of tension and incidents that leads into more violent incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Colonel, let me stop you there and ask you two specific pointed questions. You just mentioned about Travnik being the capital. Did you come to have an understanding if the Bosnian Croats wanted Travnik to be the capital of province 10?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Even though at that time it was majority Muslim municipality or a town?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And also -- you strung a series of events there together, sir. Let me ask you specifically, did you go to an Easter celebration hosted by the HVO on about the 13th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. The whole RC Zenica had been invited to attend the celebration. As we usually did, we went because we were doing the same thing for the Bosniak Muslim, when it was time for their own celebration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And among the other HVO officials present, were both Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic at this celebration?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. The invitation, if I recall correctly, came from Mr. Blaskic, but naturally all the political figures of the HVO were attending to this celebration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in the course, in fact, of that day, some of the problems became worse in Travnik, and you and other members of the ECMM left Vitez to go to -- excuse me, to Travnik to look into these problems?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. And, as a matter of fact, the situation was so intense and had deteriorated so much that even, if I recall correctly, the UNPROFOR had sent an armoured vehicle to try to establish or to provide an element of security and try to calm down the population. And in that course we naturally met the civilian police on both sides, we met the military police -- sorry, we met the army representative in Travnik on both sides, i.e. the Muslim and i.e. the Croat, and it seemed that the situation was totally out of control. Totally out of control. And in the course of it we, at the end of the day, we eventually, we had a chance with Mr. Thebault to meet with Mr. Kordic. And that was a first time that I had this opportunity to be introduced to him and to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, actually, in the course of 13th of April, at the celebration in Vitez you saw Mr. Kordic there, and then actually, when you responded to Travnik, to the problems there, you saw Mr. Kordic again in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. And we -- as I said, I mean, Ambassador Thebault engaged with them, and I came to realise then that Mr. Kordic was -- even though I knew that he was already one of the vice-presidents of the political HVO, that he was the political man at least for this Central Bosnia region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you observe of Mr. Kordic in his role that day, especially in Travnik, in relation to the other HVO officials; that is, how did he appear to relate to the other, in terms of rank or role, with the other HVO representatives there?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: As I said, he appears to be totally the political leader of the HVO. He was speaking for the whole of the Bosniak Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving on, you indicated a moment ago that part of what was happening in Travnik around this time, or did happen, was that the elected Muslim officials were being ousted from their governmental positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yeah. You must realise, that although this is one incident that I recollect clearly, but there was other incidents sometimes that were being generated too by the Muslims. But it was just an incident that generated another incident and eventually -- I mean, it became out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: But, yes, this was a very serious matter for the Bosniak Muslim, and they don't accept it and they really wanted to do something to change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me go forward. Your Honour, I think the next few paragraphs are not particularly controversial at this point in the trial, I don't think, and I will try to lead through this quite quickly. Although, with deference to the interpreters, Colonel, if you and I can both be not quite talking so fast, and if we can break between our answer and question, please. Is it correct, Colonel, that on the early morning of the 16th of April, you and another ECMM monitor were trying -- were attempting to travel from Vitez to Zenica, you got as far as Dubravica. On the way to Dubravica you found a circle of some five civilian males laying on their stomach. At first you thought these were -- that the men were dead, but as you approached and looked at them closer, you found that they were actually alive, laying on the road. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You then drove slowly back and passed them again and, in fact, passed them a third time. And around that time you saw that some soldiers, some armed soldiers in black uniforms and wearing black face masks, came out of hiding or out from the area at least and -- is that true?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you know, from your experience in Bosnia at this time, did you associate these black uniforms soldiers with something called HOS, or H-O-S?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: That's the way they were being described, so I assume that that's exactly what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you also understand that these HOS soldiers belonged to what some described as a special or special HVO units?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As you attempted to go back to these men laying on the road the third time, did the HOS soldiers open fire on you?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: As we spotted them and as they realised that we have seen them, they opened fire on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you left the area at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Sadly, yes, we had to, to leave the people on the ground to their -- by themselves, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you armed? Were you armed at the time?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: No. I mean, we were driving the armoured jeep that we had, but we -- we did pick up a few bullets on the jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you arrived at Dubravica, you tried to continue on to Zenica over the mountain road, but you were stopped by an HVO checkpoint. This checkpoint was heavily manned by HVO soldiers, in normal HVO uniforms with chequerboard patches. You were not allowed to pass the checkpoint, so you returned to Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were then stopped at an HVO checkpoint on the road to Ahmici, not far from the junction of the Ahmici road, and the main road to Zenica. This checkpoint was again heavily manned by HVO soldiers with the chequerboard patches. These soldiers would not let you proceed to the village of Ahmici, and is it correct, Colonel, that at this time it appeared to you, based on what you saw at that time driving through the Vitez area, that this entire area had been sealed off by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: That's a conclusion that we came at. But you must realise that this latest incident that you recall, that you just recalled, took place in the evening, because we were kept from moving out of Vitez. And to be able to go in front of Ahmici, we had to go to the first contact point. So later on that day we were able to go through the first roadblock. There was no -- not any longer any people there. And then we went on the route to Zenica. And that's where we saw Ahmici in flame, and that's where we saw some guards there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. During your travels around the Lasva Valley on the 16th of April, as you've described them in the last few minutes, from the morning until that evening, did you see any ABiH units or ABiH soldiers in the Vitez or Ahmici area?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: No. We saw -- we saw none of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, in terms of military personnel, the only persons you saw were these HVO or HOS soldiers?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. Mind you, though, as you recall, that we were prevented to go any further. So I don't know if they were engaging with them, but from what we saw that day and what we were allowed to see, we saw only HVO and HOS soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going on, then. On the 17th of April, did you and ECMM receive an appeal for help for the Croats living in Zenica? This was faxed to ECMM from the local HVO leadership to the BritBat commander and to RC Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if the usher could hand you Exhibits Z696 and Z723. If the usher could just put those -- those momentarily on the ELMO, please, starting with 6 -- yes, 696. Look at that document, sir. Mr. Thebault, who is one of the addressees, was the head of RC Zenica at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell, by looking at the top of that document, that in fact it was faxed from some HVO component to ECMM and BritBat on about the 17th of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You came into possession of this document during your time in Bosnia, sir?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it was given to me by Mr. Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in fact, on this exhibit, just for identification purposes, you had signed it on an earlier occasion with your name in August 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this particular communication appears to be over the name of the Minister of Defence, the secretary of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Kostroman, and the vice-president, Mr. Dario Kordic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking briefly at Exhibit 723, is that a communication from Colonel Blaskic around the same time, actually the next day, April 18th, and again did you come into possession of that document during your tour of duty in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, once again, we can see a fax strip, if you will, stripe at the top of that page coming from an HVO component; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As a result of the communications received, did you and other ECMM members undertake a series of investigations of alleged -- of these alleged complaints or protests by the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. I was tasked by Mr. Thebault to put together a small task force and try to go and physically investigate each of the known Croat villages that were around Zenica and see if, in fact, the atrocities that we were told had taken place had, in fact, taken place. So to have any credibility, we knew that we needed to have the cooperation of the Bosniak forces. We brought along the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, and then to be able to speak to the Croat people who we were going to be able to encounter and to have a visible witness -- at least credible witness with us, we brought with us Father Stjepan, who is Catholic, from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Father Stjepan is a Croat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before we get too far away from Exhibit 723, did you come to understand around this time that one of the things that the HVO officials wanted the ECMM or the International Community to do was to arrange to transport a number of Croats on buses out of Zenica and to the area around Vitez or Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, and according to what they were saying, the safety and security of all the Bosniak Croat inhabitants within the provinces that belonged to the Muslims were in great danger, and the only way and safe way to take care of it was to -- eventually was to move them from the Muslim province to the Croat province.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in connection with these investigations, you obtained the cooperation of the ABiH 3rd Corps deputy commander, Dzemal Merdan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, because there was no way for us to be able to go and visit those villages, because some of those villages were right within what we call the forward edge of the battle, the forward edge of the battle between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it your assessment at the time that you received Mr. or Colonel Merdan's full cooperation and assistance?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he's next to the -- he spent most of his time with us, allowing us to go to BiH barrage roadblocks and to allow us to go into those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And these were, in fact, to investigate alleged atrocities or events that had been carried out against the Croats by -- allegedly by the Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, Colonel, in the course of your tour of duty in Bosnia, did you ever receive any similar assistance from an HVO official to investigate alleged atrocities committed by the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It was very, very, very difficult to have this kind of assistance and to have this kind of diligent answer from the HVO. I mean whenever we wanted to visit any places that we had suspicion that a crime was committed, it took hours and hours of negotiation, and sometimes we were not able to get the necessary authority to come with us to ease the investigation. And sometimes what we had to do, we had to force our way using UNPROFOR armoured vehicles to go into the places that we wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of your investigation, did you find, in fact, that the ABiH commanders or police in the area had been told to, in fact, secure and provide for the security of what at that time were some of the abandoned Croat houses and the Croat people still living in the area?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. We saw evidence that, in fact, there was an order that had been given to try to -- considering the situation, to try to protect the goods of the Croats that were no longer staying there and to protect the Croats that were staying there. But I must say, though, that we did encounter and we did witness atrocities that had been committed against the Croats, but it definitely was not at the level which we were expecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you find that in some instances, in fact, that some of the Croats you interviewed indicated that they had been assisted and protected by their Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, and the same thing too happened in other places where Croats did protect Muslims. So, yes, we did encounter this kind of attitude from some of the Croats, saying that if it had not been for their Muslim neighbour, they would have probably been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you, in your group, in fact, witness on some occasions that BiH or Muslim military police actually arrested some people who were engaged in robbing --

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. In one instance with Father Stjepan, I think it's on the second day, as we were visiting one of the villages, we witnessed, in fact, the military police from the BiH Corps, in fact, arresting and taking away a burglar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask, in contrast, sir, did you ever see any HVO officials arrest any person in connection with the atrocities in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving on, if I can just direct your attention to Exhibit Z765, and only one question, sir. Is that a copy of a report that you prepared on, in part, some of these investigations that you have testified about in the last few minutes, a report you prepared on the 20th and the 21st of April, 1993, bearing your first name on the second page; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before changing topics, sir, what was your final assessment and ECMM's final assessment in connection with the complaints and protests that had been raised by Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic and others at that time?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, it appears at that time, as we were writing this report, that this sounds more like propaganda, okay, this sounds more alarming than, in fact, what really happened in those villages. But again I must stress that atrocity is atrocity, and we find some atrocity there. So it may be the fact that we went to investigate was an element that, in fact, allowed or forced the Bosniaks to implement safety or security measures. But definitely the alarming of the two messages that we received from the HVO, we didn't find evidence that, in fact, violence of the magnitude that they were projecting really happened, and in fact we didn't support the idea that all the Croat inhabitants of Zenica and of the neighbouring villages should be, in fact, escorted out of those areas and moved to the Croat provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to have any view whether the complaints -- the timing of the complaints on the 17th and 18th of April, the two exhibits we looked at a moment ago, had anything to do with the events in Ahmici on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, I would say that at the time we found it a bit awkward; that it seems that they already knew what had taken place in some of their villages. And yet we were to find a bit later on that other massacres that had been taking place within the Muslim area that were within the provinces, and yet we were never told that this type of violence had taken place around the same dates. And I would not be surprised to find out that a lot of the violence that erupted in the Croat-inhabited village was the result of the violence that took place in the Muslim-inhabited area that were within the province, the Croatian province.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the time that Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic sent these communications to you, did they report to you in those communications, or communications at the same time, the atrocities committed in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's move on, and if we can revert back to moving forward again rather quickly. Is it correct, sir, that you were not allowed to visit Ahmici itself until approximately the 21st of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At that time, you went to Ahmici with Ambassador Thebault. Ambassador Thebault was outraged with what he saw, made a very strong statement to a BBC news crew which was there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you become aware at that time that both Colonel Stewart and Ambassador Thebault effectively demanded an HVO investigation of atrocities in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as of the time that you left Bosnia at the end of August 1993, to your knowledge, had any HVO investigation or the results of any such investigation been reported to ECMM or the International Community, if you know?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher could just briefly put before you Exhibits 1592.1 through 1592.6.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, according to our records, these are additional exhibits that have not previously been produced to us by the scheduled deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I suppose that's correct, Your Honour. The witness tendered them. We thought they had been sent before. We found yesterday that, in fact, for whatever reason, they had not previously been received, and they were copied again, which we believed to be a second time, yesterday. But it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They are photographs, so they are usually admitted. But let us take this as quickly as we can. We've had a great deal of evidence about Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, and I was not going to -- other than to have, Your Honour, the witness authenticate his photographs, I was not going to go any further. If you can simply show them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are those photographs, sir, that you took in Ahmici on or about the 21st of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Two very final questions -- two quick questions on Ahmici. When you were there on the 21st of April, did you see any defensive positions, military positions, in the village?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you see anything, in your military experience, about the village or anything you saw in the village at that time which indicated that an attack on that village would have had a military purpose?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the 21st of April, did there continue to be any substantial HVO military presence in the village?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: All I recall is that we had to be provided escort by BritBat to be able to be allowed to visit the village. That's the only -- to my recollection, the entrance was being guarded by a normal roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As a professional infantry officer, what significance, if any, would it have to you that only several days after an attack of this magnitude, there would be no forces of the conquering side still in the village?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It was significant. I mean I'm still even being -- wondering exactly what was the objective, if it was a military objective. What we saw and what we can describe briefly was just the work of the -- what we call the cleaning-up operation. Okay. What they wanted to do was just to clean up the village from all of its inhabitants. But as far as tactical gain, I cannot see what was the tactical gain of this village compared to the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your military experience, as one side takes a particular village or location, is it more typical that forces would be left in that village to maintain the control of the area they just, if you will, conquered?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward. On the 19th of April of 1993, were you in Zenica, sir?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Sorry, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. On the 19th of April, 1993, were you in your hotel in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I would tend to say, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident about that time where approximately six artillery shells fell on the centre of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's very clear. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After that point in time, I take it, sir, that you were not involved in investigating that particular shelling, but that was carried out by other ECMM monitors?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to know a Bosnian Croat military officer named Franjo Nakic?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you relate to the Court, very briefly, what observations, if any, you have concerning Mr. Nakic -- was he Colonel Blaskic's, for a time, deputy commander in the Central Bosnia operative zone?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: That's the way that he was introduced to me on the Busovaca Joint Commission, as being the HVO Croat representative. And his counterpart was Mr. Merdan. And that's the type of level of authority that we needed to have in this Busovaca Joint Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you become aware, in about the middle of April 1993, that Mr. Nakic was removed or effectively relieved of his authority as deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yeah, we've been trying to get in touch with him to find him finally at his home. And he seems to be, during all this crisis, the mid of April, he was at his residence. And I found out later on that he had been given the job of chief of staff, but in fact he didn't have any longer any authority within the HVO central forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your dealings with the various HVO officials in Central Bosnia during your tour of duty, would you have considered Mr. Nakic to be a moderate?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I would think so, yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to have any information whether Mr. Nakic had some objection or protest to what he saw going on?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, but that's the only explanation that I could come to grasp, to explain why he had been relieved of his duty in the midst of a major crisis, and yet be reintegrated in a former or lower position within the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On about the 18th of April 1993 -- while I am asking the question, if the usher could please put before the witness Exhibit 719. On the 18th of April, did you have a meeting with again the ABiH 3rd Corps deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that involved, in part, a discussion of what he considered the Croat aims or objectives to be in Central Bosnia at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exhibit 719, in part -- well, is it a report that you prepared and signed on the last page, and does it include notes or a description of this meeting with the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to item number 4 on the second page. Do you recall that the specific role of Mr. Kordic was involved, or was discussed?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is a reference to some dealings between Mr. Kordic and the Serb leader Karadzic. Were you ever able to confirm that, in fact, there had been some dealings or communications between Mr. Kordic and Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: No, I was not able to confirm that, in fact, this incident took place, but it became obvious at a certain point in time that there had been definitely some kind of agreement between the Serbs and the Croats. And this was reported in another report to the effect that, for example, Croat people were being transported through Serb lines and eventually were being sent back to the Croat area. And to be able to do this, I mean, there was only one way that, in fact, some kind of understanding had been taking place between the two sides. And at the same time too, later on we realised that the front line between the Croats and the Serbs on the west side had been moved, and had been providing tactical advantages to the Serbs. And again, without having to fight for it. And that became obvious to us, that something had happened at that time or during those days so as to allow this kind of activity to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Going forward, sir. Around the 22nd of April 1993, were ECMM monitors involved in investigating the status of eight Muslim villages in the Kiseljak municipality, and did they find that these eight villages had been largely or totally destroyed with many Muslims killed and mistreated?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, maybe not totally destroyed, but we were able to investigate that atrocity had taken place. And what I would say, atrocity take place through the type of -- using the HOS technique, which was, for example, in a village, if you had a Croat house, a Muslim house, well, it was quite obvious that, as we were investigating, that some of the Muslim houses had been burnt to the ground, while nothing happened to the Croat houses. And then I myself investigated one area where civilians had been decapitated, had been burned alive, raped, and then executed, and then the whole, the rest of the whole population was being kept at the end of the village in more or less a kind of -- I would not say a gaol, but they were limited to stay there, with almost no water, no -- nothing to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was the village of Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: That was the village of Rotilj, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we get to Rotilj. For the record, the other eight or the other seven of these villages, did they include Svinjarevo, Jehovac, Behrici, Gomionica, Gromiljak, Hercezi, Dolci, the Muslim part of Polje Visnjica, and again, as you said, Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, as it was reported on the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And consistent with some of your testimony earlier, did you find that the ECMM -- did the ECMM find that their access into a number of these villages was initially blocked or prevented by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. In the case of the village that I visited myself, we were kept from using the road. So we had to leave our vehicles some kilometres away from that central post and then use a mountain road or go across -- across to eventually to be able to have access to the village. And in the other instances I know that my colleague, if it would not have been from the support of the UNPROFOR, would not have had access to those villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, we are going to adjourn for ten minutes. If you could try and shorten the rest of the evidence, as far as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Nice indicates that he would like to have a quick private session after Court. (Private Session)

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. 4.00, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will move very quickly on and, with the Court's permission, except for those portions which touch specifically on Mr. Kordic, move quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On Rotilj, your investigation there showed that approximately seven Muslims had been killed, with substantial destruction in the village. You learned this information, in part, from interviewing two Muslims, Muslim villagers, who gave detailed -- one of them, in fact, was the spouse of one of the murdered villagers. And there were actually a few Croats in the area who also confirmed the massacre, and, of course, also confirmed by other Muslims; is that true?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is true, and as far as for some of the victims, we were able to see the stain, the blood stain, either on the house -- for example, the lady that was raped and then killed, we could see evidence that it had just recently happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The information reported to you indicated that approximately 20 HVO soldiers had attacked Rotilj on the 18th and 19th of April, 1993, burnt down approximately 19 Muslim houses, also some barns and other buildings. Again seven Muslims were executed. The village was not defended by the ABiH, based on the information known to you, with any elements or members of those forces instead deployed to the Visoko area. Some of the houses were looted before being burnt down. In contrast, none of the Croat houses in the village were damaged. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The seven persons who were killed and the reported circumstances of their deaths were -- Zibiza Skrso, a 31-year-old, was raped and then killed by small-arms fire. You could still see evidence of the rape and blood stains in the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Another victim was Miralem Topalovic, 43 years old, and Esad Topalovic, 28 years old, both killed by having their heads split open, were found laying on the side of the road; Bajro Pusculovic, 63 years old, and Zila Pusculovic, 61 years old, both reportedly burnt alive in their house. Devad Hodic, 26 years old, was murdered, and Zijad Kosovac, 16 years old, was murdered. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it also part of your investigation that it was shown that on the next morning after the attack, and that was on the 18th and 19th of April, that many of the older or younger Muslim men were arrested and taken to an HVO prison in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you wrote a report on this investigation, which is Exhibit Z818, and unless there's some question by the Defence, Your Honour, I'll simply move on. I think it's available and can be reviewed with the witness, if the Defence wishes. You had indicated, before the break in your testimony, that Rotilj itself was later used as something of a detention camp. Is it correct, sir, that given the topography and access into the village, that a relatively small number of HVO soldiers could essentially control egress and -- strike that -- could control access into and out of the village?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when used as a detention camp, the conditions in the village of Rotilj were found to be not satisfactory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, is it correct, Colonel, that the events you've testified about today, primarily in the Vitez/Busovaca/Kiseljak area and, I suppose, Travnik as well, were the events that you saw happening limited to those areas, or did you, in fact, see other similar events taking place in other parts of Bosnia, including such places as Prozor, Gornji Vakuf and Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see physically what was taking place in Prozor or Jablanica, but since we had an ECMM monitor in the neighbourhood, we were able to get a copy of their report, which indicated that there was some fighting going on and sometimes heavy fighting going on in that area. In those areas, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as reported to ECMM, again, did many of the events in these areas involve Muslim civilians suffering from various HVO actions, with the HVO components again in those areas preventing often UNPROFOR and ECMM from entering the areas?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can just have the witness -- on this one I will pause long enough to have the witness shown Exhibit 692.1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that a copy, sir, of an ECMM --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in the same category. It's never been produced to us before, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct. It was produced by the witness since he's arrived here, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's it about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's about, as the witness just testified, about attacks in the Gornji Vakuf, Prozor and Jablanica area, which were happening at the same time as the attacks in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Sayers, I don't think you will be cross-examining here today after all, so you will have time to look at it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it the conclusion of the ECMM whether these various attacks on these various locations were random or isolated, or was it your assessment that they were part of an overall strategy or plan?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Our feeling was that they were part of a grand strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you find, during your tour of duty in Bosnia, that the HVO leadership often used the giving or withholding of humanitarian aid as a weapon or tool to accomplish objectives?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: On numerous occasions, since they were controlling mainly the major access route to Central Bosnia and, as you recall, one of the prime missions of UNPROFOR was eventually to deliver food and supplies. So on numerous occasions they used roadblocks to prevent or to delay the delivery of those goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the 28th of April 1993. Was there a meeting about that day involving, perhaps among others, Ambassador Thebault, HVO General Petkovic, Colonel Blaskic, and the ABiH Commander Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that you recall that the meeting began in a bad atmosphere, with General Petkovic setting preconditions for any cooperation from the HVO; the meeting about that time was interrupted by a BritBat report that the HVO had attacked and hijacked some 40 trucks of an UNHCR humanitarian aid convoy of food?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would appreciate it if the Prosecution wouldn't lead on the next few paragraphs up to paragraph 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Not intended.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I just want to correct that the convoy was not attacked, but was just taken as hostage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you relate to the Court, please, in your own words, just the series of events, then, that took place in connection with the release -- obtaining the release of this convoy?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: As the meeting was going on with Ambassador Thebault, I myself was the desk officer in the ops room, and I received the call and I am the one that more or less interrupted Ambassador Thebault to let him know about this crisis. What followed was a series of contact, because we realised that the Busovaca Brigade, HVO brigade commander was the one that had orchestrated this crisis by taking the convoy hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you, sir. Just for the record, this HVO brigade commander was named Dusko Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in the course of your tour in Bosnia, had you had prior dealings?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So Mr. Grubesic was somebody you knew?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead and continue, please.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: And then eventually, since we were talking about a ceasefiring agreement, that we were talking about implementing the Vance-Owen Plan, it comes to -- the HVO commander comes to realise that there was something wrong going on. So both of them, Colonel Blaskic and General Petkovic, attempted to have the brigade commander release the convoy. And in both instances they were told that the brigade commander at that time had received specific orders by Mr. Kordic, and they were not going to execute the order coming from a normal chain of command. And I recall that after other discussions, that finally they went through the political network, and eventually they had -- were able to contact, I gather, Mr. Kordic, and had the brigade commander release the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The brigade that Mr. Grubesic was the commander of was the Busovaca Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You indicated a moment ago that you were in, I think, the operations room, is that correct, while this was going on?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you present when General Petkovic and Colonel Blaskic were involved in communications to attempt to get the convoy released?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I was present, but they were speaking in Serbo-Croat, and my Serbo-Croat is not that good to understand exactly what they were saying, but our interpreter said they, in fact, were attempting to get in touch with the brigade commander, and it was very clear that he was not going to obey their order, which was to eventually to release the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to hear or were you informed during this time whether this brigade commander had -- my question is a little different, so please listen specifically. Not that he only would release the convoy on the order of a particular person, but did he indicate that the original hijacking or taking of the convoy had been on the order of a particular person?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's a leading question, I believe, Your Honour, and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I haven't suggested an answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: What was very clear to me is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. No, I think the question is acceptable. Yes. If you'd like to answer it. If you can remember what it was.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, what was very clear is that neither Colonel Blaskic nor General Petkovic at the time appeared to be aware of what was going on. And what appeared very clear at that time is that the brigade commander of Busovaca had received specific orders, and what appears to be very clear is that he mentioned through again our translator that he was taking his order from Mr. Kordic, at least specifically for that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Colonel, is it your experience and training and to your knowledge true of most armies in the world that the military forces ultimately come under the control of political officials?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Usually. Usually that's what is taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you, with the usher's assistance, to be shown Exhibits 840 and 857.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Exhibit Z857.3 has never been produced by the deadline set in the timetabling order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe this one was, Your Honour. It was not produced today or by Mr. Landry. It came to us some time ago. And I believe it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the significance of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is a BritBat report, Your Honour, that is, in part -- if the Court will give me one moment, please. Confirms, if you will, this particular incident. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Yes, on page 2, under the -- under the item C, Central Bosnia. You can see that and the comment that follows, Your Honour. And Z840 has been produced earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Z840 has been produced, Z857.3 has not, and we object to it on the grounds of untimely disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we think it was. Without having specific records in front of us, it's been produced to us for some days. It was not a document produced by Mr. Landry since arriving here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think it's timely and I think it's actually a document in which there has been certainly reference to this particular event, if not this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This matter can be resolved in this way. Tomorrow you will tell us what -- when it was that it was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I don't think there is any prejudice in letting it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can just continue then. If I can direct your attention, sir, to 840. Directing your attention to the bottom of the second page under item numbered 3. The paragraph starting with the, "They asked thereafter for a common meeting." And if you just look at that section, and carrying over onto the next page. Was that consistent -- is that a report, in part, about the very event that you've testified about in the last few minutes?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And subject to our clarification, Your Honour, if I can just ask the witness's opinion in connection with, again, Exhibit 857.3, item C on the second page, item C2, BHC report. Does that also appear to you to be an accurate report, if you will, of this event concerning the 40-vehicle UNHCR convoy?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, our case manager indicates that this document was sent on the 1st of February, 1993. I'm sorry, why do I say that? I think we have "'93" on the brain, Your Honour. I'm sorry. The 1st of February, 2000. I think it was -- in looking at the BritBat, there were a handful of BritBat documents that came in on a Monday as opposed to the previous Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So this is 857, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Point 3, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward, then, very quickly on the Convoy of Joy, Colonel, because the Court has heard, I can report to you, I think, extensive testimony about that, did you understand that this very large convoy, at the end of May and early June of 1993, had been allowed by the International Community, in part, based on the HVO promise or guarantee that security would be provided by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any additional evidence this witness can give about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: About only one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you specifically again in the operations room of the ECMM in Zenica while the events of the Convoy of Joy, in particular regarding when various attacks on the convoy were taking place, were you in the operations room?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I was directly involved with the preparation of this convoy, with the conduct of this convoy and in the aftermath of this convoy, and most of -- and as the convoy was being -- was moving initially from Tuzla to the south part of Bosnia and then back, I was operating the ops centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. One or two final questions on it. If the witness can be shown Exhibit Z1045.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention, Colonel, to about three fourths of the way down the first page -- well, first of all, this is a reference to the Tuzla food convoy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that also known as the Convoy of Joy?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And about three-fourths of the way down the first page -- and by the way, on the second page -- I'm sorry, I'm getting out of turn here. The second page, this is your report signed with your name, "Remi Landry"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Back to the first page, about three-fourths of the way down, did you report that after a contact with M. Kordic, he promised his help for --

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: All I can say is that if it's written there -- I have no precise recollection, but all I can say is I did write this report, and if it's there, that's what took place, to the effect that personally I did contact him or somebody from the ECMM or RC Zenica contacted. That is the best of my recollection for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Did you and ECMM, sir, have the -- take the position or reach the conclusion, in about June of 1993, that there were HV, that is, Croatian army troops or elements, operating on Bosnian territory, providing logistical support to HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, and this was not just coming from us. We had suspicions since a long time that the HV forces were giving them a hand in the Prozor/Jablanica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it your assessment or view that one of the things the HV troops did to attempt to avoid detection was to make their movements usually at night?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, and the reason is very simple, is that we were not allowed to move at night because of security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was the policy of ECMM?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It was a policy of ECMM within Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At various times in your career, sir, you've been an intelligence officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you -- during your tour of duty in Bosnia, is it fair to say that based on the information available to you and ECMM, that there was an assessment made of a close link between the Zagreb government and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can just briefly tell the Court what you base that on, what your conclusion was and what you base that on.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, our conclusion again, as I've said earlier, that we were aware or that we had good suspicion to believe that there was some kind of agreement that took place between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic about splitting Bosnia in two parts, and later on it became quite obvious that the people that we had in the Prozor area started to report intense activity, that, in fact, that activity was military activity, and that could not have been initiated or have come from within Bosnia-Herzegovina but had to come from the Split area. And as you know, Split was part of Croatia. Later on, on one of my trips, I was myself able to identify logistic units that were in the area of Prozor that didn't belong to HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As a professional military officer, Colonel, is it true that logistical support is absolutely vital to any military operation?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is vital, without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it ECMM's assessment that the HV or Croatian army was providing substantial logistical support to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the course of your duties, did it come to your attention that HV General Praljak, in fact, at one point had acknowledged that there were HV troops in Bosnia along a ceasefire line, at least in particular regard -- excuse me -- with a ceasefire line south-west of Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. If I recall correctly, there was a few papers that circulated more or less confirming the doubt that we have about providing logistical support.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to have information that there were HV troops or HV elements involved in supporting the HVO fight against the Muslims, who were involved in HVO offensive operations in the area between Mostar and Jablanica and Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: You have to realise that we had a very strong suspicion that this was taking place, but we were not allowed to go into this area to further investigate. So our feeling is that it would be -- it is possible that HV forces would provide not only logistical support to HVO, but it would make sense -- much more sense that the units that were potentially provided by the HV forces would require extensive logistical support and that logistical support could be based in the area of Prozor or nearby to support any further actions that were taking place further to the east towards Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your military judgement, based on what you saw during your time in Bosnia, did the HVO have the type of logistical support or resources to mount the kind of operations that you saw being mounted without substantial outside support?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It's a very difficult question. All I can say is that I didn't see any of the type of heavy equipment or armoured vehicle in Central Bosnia that would have required the type of logistical support that we saw deployed in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So just so the record -- if I understand you correctly, sir, you saw such activity that would support that kind of involvement in Prozor, but not so much in around the area, say, of Vitez or Busovaca or something like that?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. And, in fact, just so the record is clear, you did not personally see HV troops specifically in Vitez, Busovaca, or Kiseljak during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you see any HVO units, equipment, or supplies anywhere in Bosnia during -- yourself while there?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: HVO equipment? Yes, I saw some definitely in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. HV or HVO?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I didn't see any HV equipment in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I did see HVO equipment in Central Bosnia. I did see HV logistic equipment in the area of Prozor, but I didn't see any HV fighting vehicles or fighting units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Did you understand the control of the HDZ/HVO leadership in Central Bosnia to extend to such places as Zepce and Vares?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. According to the aide-memoire that we were being provided by UNPROFOR and that were being reviewed on a regular basis, okay, those locations were under the command of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Specifically, sir, in terms of the more traditional, if you will, regular soldier military leader, is it fair to say that that was Colonel Blaskic in that -- in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, throughout my stay, he posed himself as being the senior officer of HVO forces within Central Bosnia and, as such, the force commander within Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where did you see, if any, Mr. Kordic fit into the leadership structure in central -- in that same area called Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, he was -- at that time his name was posted as being the vice-president of the political party, and as such living in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you relate to the Court, perhaps, any particular description yourself that you've used, and that maybe was used at ECMM, to describe the view or assessment of Mr. Kordic's role? There may be some vernacular term that --

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, let's say that it was well known and well shared within the UNPROFOR community, within the ECMM community, that Mr. Kordic was the political master of Central Bosnia. He was the authority, as far as any political decision that had to be taken for the future of the Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of concepts of command and control, sir, are you familiar, both with your own army's doctrine, and also what at one time would have been the Warsaw Pact doctrine in connection with the responsibility of military commanders in terms of their control and punishment of their own forces?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
