utterances.text: During your time in Central Bosnia, did either Colonel Blaskic or any other senior HVO official indicate to you that in any large scale sort of way they did not have command and control over their units and troops?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. Mind you, though, it was well-known that because of the communication equipment, because of the fact that their army was not a professional army, that at times they were not having the full control of all the action of all of their troops. But throughout -- I mean, they never deny the fact that they posted themselves as being the overall commander of the HVO forces within Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, just so your testimony is clear, when you talk about such events, that there could have been some instances of uncontrolled elements, in your assessment could such uncontrolled elements been responsible for some event on the size or magnitude of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: No, definitely not. And as I've mentioned earlier -- I mean, the whole area was sealed by HVO forces, and they were uniformed with the regular HVO uniforms. So it appears to me that this has been well orchestrated, and those people had received specific orders to seal this area as atrocity or as they were burning down the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would your assessment be much the same for the attacks and events that you also described in the Kiseljak area?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Mind you, though, that the only reason I would say yes, is the fact that not necessarily each of those incident itself were in the magnitude of what took place in Ahmici, but the fact that they all took place at about the same time. I found it a bit unusual to have so many troops out of control, that would decide to pick a village and then to do this kind of atrocity at the same time. So I would tend to say that for that reason, that those type of incidents had been orchestrated to -- at the higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did it come to your attention, at any time during your tour in Bosnia, that you saw any disciplinary action taken or criminal Prosecution taken by the Bosnian Croat authorities against anyone accused of what might be called a war crime?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. And the thing that we were all looking for was following the incident of the crisis in Busovaca, we were wondering if, in fact, the brigade commander would be relieved of his post, but nothing happened, at least not to our knowledge. And he remains a brigade commander there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You are talking now about the reference to the brigade commander who would not act to release the convoy, except on Mr. Kordic's orders?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Even though one might say his more normal military chain of command might have been, for instance, Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know if the officer known as Grubesic, was he ever punished or relieved of command for insubordination?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: That's what I was alluding to, that we were expecting that some disciplinary measure might have been taken but, to the best of our knowledge, nothing took place, because he kept his brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in fact, after this incident, did you, sir, continue to have dealings with Officer Grubesic before you left Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I might, but this is not -- I cannot really recall having met him after. I know that I have met him during this period, but specifically I don't recall -- I base my judgement or my statement here on the fact that his name remained throughout that period as the brigade -- as being posted on the UNPROFOR aide-memoire as being the brigade commander for that Busovaca Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And continued to be after the --

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: So that if something had happened, his name would have been replaced, as it was the case with brigade commanders that were being replaced, that were being promoted to other functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: One final question, Colonel. During your time in Bosnia, can you tell the Court what your observation was in terms of the status, if you will, or future of a military commander who was seen as not acting consistent with the plans and strategies of his or her political leader?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, usually it didn't take long, that those individuals that show or manifested this kind of uncooperative attitude were sacked. They were removed from command. And I have examples on both side, that an individual suddenly disappeared because, according to their master, they were not fully in agreement or they were not capable of fulfilling the task that they were being given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can just have a moment. One moment. Just to finish up, I missed one exhibit. If the usher could show you Exhibit 901.2. And if I can anticipate Mr. Sayers, Your Honour. I think this document was produced the same time as the earlier BritBat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The same objection, Your Honour. It wasn't produced by January the 28th, which was a date set in the timetabling order for the delivering to us of all exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then again, Your Honour, I would say that we were in communication with the British MOD, we had hoped to have certain documents faxed to us. The calendar will show that the 28th was a Friday and the 1st was a Monday and, unfortunately, a handful of documents didn't get to us until the following Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The position is that the Defence have had this a month, therefore it's admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Colonel, final -- I guess with this exhibit the final question. If I can direct your attention to page 6. The item number 3, "personalities." If you can just -- if you'll just read that to yourself, personalities, item A, and the following comment. And my last question is: Is that assessment consistent with your own assessment and ECMM's assessment as to the role played by Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: All I can say is that we -- as I've said earlier, I mean, we knew that Mr. Kordic was a very powerful man within Central Bosnia, and we knew that Colonel Blaskic was the one that was more or less commanding the troops. And we knew that there was definitely direct links between Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic. I would not say it in the way that it has been expressed by the owner of this document, but, yes, I would tend to agree with what is being said there, but not -- would not express it the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You wouldn't choose those words?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I wouldn't choose those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you help us with tomorrow. We had at one stage thought of sitting at 9.00, but from what you say, you think it's going to be rather unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Subject to the length of the cross-examination of this witness, I would have thought that the cross-examination of the other witness could easily be accomplished within an ordinary Court day, and any balance of time could probably or possibly be used for the exhibits exercise. There may be other procedural matters, but I don't think they are likely to take very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, there is no reason, is there, why we shouldn't get through some cross-examination, sufficient cross-examination in the morning to finish another witness during the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't anticipate that there will be a problem with that at all, especially in light of the accelerative instructions I was given today. I don't think that my cross-examination of Colonel Landry should last longer than the morning, and maybe less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we sit at half past 9, that should be sufficient, should it? Very well, we'll sit at half past 9 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I trouble the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Contrary to earlier indications. Yes, we'll rise for five minutes. Colonel, would you be back, please, tomorrow at half past 9 for cross-examination, and we'll finish your evidence then. Could you remember not, please, to speak to anybody during the course of this adjournment about your evidence until it's over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, we'll adjourn for an ex parte hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
